At first I thought it was just my fault. Perhaps I put loaded them in the dishwasher in the wrong way. Perhaps I cracked them by mistake and did not realize...but now, having only five left (and we ordered three large boxes of them! So initially we had over 30 jars) I finally have come to the conclussion that this is simply a MANUFACTURING FLAW.

All of other sizes, which we use in similar manner to the larger jars, are fine. None of them has ever cracked. Only the larger ones.

I thought we were making an investment on buying American made quality. I am so very very sad to have thrown so much money in the trash by purchasing these larger size jars. Again, at least three large boxes of the large jars. That's quite a bit of money to toss into the recycling bin.

So, no, NO, NO, I would NOT recommend the large size.

Extremely disappointed.. [[VIDEOID:60b3421b37e146146d8ec5101f5d2b2]] This kit seems to be on a deal due to some issues with the brown keg that's included in the kit.
I am an AVID Mr. Beer fan since these smaller kegs are easier to use and allows a new brewer to experiment with smaller batches (versus a 5+ gallon batch).
The spout helps limit the need for a bottling bucket.
I have not had a leak issue with any other Mr. Beer kits (I have 3 Mr Beer kegs currently).
I received this kit and was going to prove to other reviewers that it was merely a spigot issue rather than a faulty keg issue.
I sanitized the brown keg with the sanitizer in the sink and didn't notice any real issues.
I filled the keg with cold water and began the brew process.
I noticed some water on the counter but figured it was just runoff from the sanitizing solution I had poured out.
Once the boil was all done I was ready to cool the wort and put in the keg but there was even more water. I picked up the keg and saw that along the seam on the bottom of the brown fermenter there was water dripping out rather steadily.
I had the brew all mixed up so I then sanitized and leak checked the clear fermenter and there are no issues.
I'm hoping to get some form of refund or replacement keg from Amazon/Mr Beer as this is extremely disappointing.
THOROUGHLY check your fermenter before starting anything. Put a towel underneath just to be safe during the leak check, otherwise you may be initially fooled as I was.
Check out the video for the leak issue.

I have city water which is well treated but I wanted something to get the chlorine and such out- apparently this just isn't an option for us. Going back to our Brita filter that has a filter that lasts a year and you just change out the charcoal puck filter every now and again. It filters chlorine and such out of it and isn't zero tds but it's more sustainable price wise and the water tastes better than this zero stuff.

Water Water Everywhere...and Only a Drop of Coffee to Drink.. One thing about this coffeemaker is that it will certainly help keep your countertops clean since it's nearly impossible to fill without spilling water everywhere. The design of the caraffe, while looking perfectly normal, is amazingly bad. Water pours down the caraffe & off the bottom every time. Maybe I'll someday master the technique of pouring water into the coffeemaker, but I don't often have the delicate skills of a brain-surgeon when I roll out of bed in the morning and stumble toward the kitchen.

Secondly, the maker does come with a permanent wire coffee basket, but I've never used it because it's so small. Perhaps it would work for most people, but I like my coffee a little on the strong side and the basket seems tiny. The good news is that you can still use paper filters in the coffeemaker, but the bad news is that you still have to use paper filters.

If space is a consideration, please be aware that the top of the coffeemaker is all one solid piece that lifts from the front. This means you need to have clearance above the maker that at least equals the depth of the appliance from front to back. My old 4-cup maker fit perfectly under a cabinet, but this one doesn't quite fit in the same space. Certainly it's no fault of the appliance, but I wish I'd realized it beforehand.

Lastly, a note to Southpaws. The lift-out coffee basket has a flat tab on the backside that serves, I guess, as a handle. The basket only fits one way, with the flat tab extending over the left side of the water resevoir. Lefties pouring water into the maker will have a difficult time missing the tab that sticks out over the water resevoir, and pouring water on the tab causes it to splash everywhere or pour down onto the hotplate area. It's probably not a good idea to lay your cell phone down anywhere around this coffeemaker.

The Longest "10 Minutes" Ever. After a year, I'm going back to a different coffee maker. This Bunn takes forever to brew a pot of coffee. It's ok if you're one of those very organized people who can remember to set up the Bunn the night before to brew automatically before you wake up, but for people like me, who stumble to the coffee pot in the morning and need some as quickly as possible, it's a pain.

The Phase Brew takes so long because it heats all the water up to the right temp before sending any of it through the coffee grounds, but, honestly, while that all sounds good, I can't tell one bit of difference between all the water being heated up first, and any other coffee pot that simply sends the water through as it is heating. I think it's just a gimmick and a selling point that actually means very little for the consumer.

Another problem is that the "clean" indicator, that tells when the maker needs to be cleaned, goes off all the time. As other long-term users review this brewer, you'll see that this happens a lot, and Bunn claims it's because of local power grids. Well, I don't have any control over the local power grid, so I can only exercise what control I do have by buying a reasonably-priced brewer that actually works when I need it to work.

****Update as of 6/30/13****

I eventually returned this unit to Bunn after they agreed that there was a defect with the cleaning indicator, and they sent a replacement very quickly. Customer service was terrific, but the replacement had the same problem as the first model. If I'd been diligent and called them again, I'm sure they would have sent another replacement, but I'm not diligent. I'm a lazy internet shopper, and it was easier to just buy a tried & true workhorse brand brewer for every day use and use the French press for something special occasions.

Wet Cat Rug. Close your eyes. No, wait, open them, I need you to keep reading or this won't work. So, keep your eyes open, but kind of act like they should be closed. Better. Now, imagine yourself stepping out of the shower. It smells amazing. (You just went to LUSH, so this was quite possibly a holy experience here.) You feel great. You grab your towel. It is perfectly dried, still smells a little like your fabric softener but is that perfect towel feel. Everything is perfect. Then you step on a wet cat! Wait. What? You look down, hoping your cat isn't really under your feet. Nope. Just this rug. This cat fur rug. That looked so super chic when you placed it in front of the shower. It looked great with my coral honeycomb pattern shower curtain. A perfect postmodern mesh. But wet cat feel just ruined the shower experience. You try to figure out how to get off the wet cat rug. You figure you'll just finish drying off, since it is a bathroom rug and will certainly at least absorb the water rolling off your body. You'd be wrong, again. Wet cat is surprisingly unabsorbent. So after your shower, you have to dry the floor, since the wet cat proved worthless at his job. But at least he looks snazzy. No? No. He looks like a wet cat laying in front of your shower. A mangled wet dumpster cat. This is bad. Maybe when it dries it will be better? A little. But not the chic look you had before. Now your cat is dry, but has some odd cowlicks he didn't have before. Who thought faux fur would be a good idea in a bathroom? And why did I think it'd be a good idea? Did no one stop and say, "Hey, this might feel awful when wet and look like a wet cat?" I mean, I didn't. But I don't get paid to make cat rugs.

Craftsman drop leaf microwave cart. Builder beware! I'm giving it a single star based on the difficulty of assembly. The finished product, however, looks sturdy and cute. So, appearance and functionality can bring it up to three or four stars, based on one's needs.

Positive: I suspect that the Catskill Craftsmen microwave cart 7222N would fit nicely in a small kitchen or apartment. It's cute and very compact.

Functionality: Without the flaps, the top counter is 17 3/4W x 19 3/4D, the right size for a 7.0 cu.ft. microwave oven. Each flap adds an additional 10 ¾ inches of width on each side, providing a total of 39.25 inches, not the manufacturer's description of forty inches.

The inside of the drawer is 2 3/8 inches high, nice height for storing recipes or small utensils. The shelf under the drawer is 16Wx17 ¼ Dx6 1/2H. The shelf behind the two doors measures is 14 ¾ H from its floor to the magnetic metal strike plate. Shelf width is compromised about one and half inches plus because of the 3/4 inch doors and clearance swing space of each door, making the entrance of that bottom shelf slightly narrower than the top shelf.

I bought this cart as a TV stand because TV stands are usually too low; I like the added height. However, the bottom shelves are too narrow to house my DVDR/VCR, so I'll install a TV monitor stand on the top shelf, adding an extra five to seven inches to the cart's overall height. With or without the flaps,it's fine for my small 22" monitor's stand which is narrower than the momitor.

I purchased this Catskill kit because it was primarily described as hardwood. It is hardwood for the important parts: the counter and both leaves, entire drawer, two doors, the three cross slats, and the four posts that hold the unit up. The back, the two sides, the shelves and the two smaller slats that hold the drawer slides are fiberboard (particle board). However, once the unit is assembled, it resembles 100% hardwood.

The wheels are sturdy and spin easily, making it easy to push the cart about. It has two lock wheels in front where they are easily accessible if you are facing the cart. However, they will work easily well if they are placed on right or left side of cart.

Negative: It's a pain in the neck to assemble and the finished unit looks too small, especially the doors.
Over the years, I've assembled numerous Saunder and O'Sullivan units (bookcases, desks, microwave cart, and bedroom furniture) with very clear instructions and easy assembly. This unit was not easy to put together.

My pet peeve was with the tiny recesses that house the nuts that hold the twelve bolts to the mainframe. I couldn't get a good hold with a small wrench or the needle nose pliers. My neighbor happened to arrive as I was struggling with one of those nuts. To no avail, he tried holding the nuts with his fingers (something I had already attempted). He couldn't get his finger in the hole. Delicate thin fingers would have worked fine, but we don't fit that profile. Another remedy is to assemble the unit on its side, but if you are a big person or have limited mobility it will be difficult to assemble the second side in that manner because the cart is very narrow. We finally resorted to using a small flat screwdriver at the proper angle, and, to our chagrin, the nuts slipped off numerous times before we could get them to mate with each bolt.

The drawer's two bastion posts, and the doors' four pins were also a pain in the neck. In the instructions, it doesn't say how far the four pins should be hammered into the predrilled holes. I hammered them in too far, leaving about ¼ inch protruding from each slot, and we had to struggle to get them out another ¼ inch each. The extra length was needed in order to prevent the doors from falling out of the mainframe.

Where to place the drawer's cabinet side glides was another guessing game because each side gets two screws and there are four predrilled holes. One schematic shows the glides' placement close to the front edge and the other displays them further in. The location of the door magnet was the final guessing game; there were no predrilled holes for it or the matching plate.

You don't need to flip the heavy cabinet twice, as instructed. I purposely assembled the unit upside down, permitting me to do a single flip after it was completely assembled.

In addition to the suggested tools, hammer, flat and Phillips screwdrivers, and pliers, you will need thin fingers or a very narrow ¼ inch wrench, a rubber mallet and a lot of patience handling those nuts. I've learned that it would be nice to see the assembly specs before purchasing any unit, especially when you're buying on-line.

But first, I'll mentioned that I read EC's review, where he trashes this jar opener, which broke in two when he tried to adjust it over a Costco jar that has a wide lid. He goes on to recommend it for grammy and people with arthritis. I don't know how he arrived at that conclusion, since people with arthritis need more help than people without that crippling affliction, which I have. So, if this piece of junk doesn't work for people with normal hands, don't expect it to work for anyone else. I often search for items that will help me and that can also be adapted for other purposes. After overlooking this particular jar opener numerous times because it reminds me of similar poorly designed models that I've seen at Sears and dollar stores, I decided to give it a test run. It was definitely a bad decision; I should have listened to my intuition.

Length 9 1/8". Largest jar opening: a deceptive 3". Smallest opening: a deceptive 1 1/4". I say deceptive because that is what one perceives while the opener is attached to its cardboard retainer. You are also deceived into thinking that the grip is an inch deep when, in truth, it's only 3/8" (less than half an inch) as the inner part of the opening grip loses 5/8" of hold, making it fit unevenly over any jar you try to open, causing slipping and perhaps harm to your hands. In short, it's more than junk. It's a catastrophe!

I've read and written enough reviews to know old reviews for a good product could remain at a website long after the manufacturer decides to skimp on quality and produce an inferior model. The retailer or manufacturer's associates, paid reviewers, and friends might also submit reviews that are less than truthful. So, the reader reads an excellent review and ends up with a lousy product. I've seen such deterioration with Fiskars scissors, the Vitality toothbrush, and a Pentel pen. Somehow, I suspect that this jar opener was always terrible.

For arthritic hands and in order of preference I've had good results with the following jar openers: the wrench strap style called Power Grip [[ASIN:B000ZSH3BQ Power Grip Jar Opening System from Handy Trends (2 PACK) As Seen on TV]]. I bought a small 4" long nameless version of this junky Easi-Twistjar opener at the dollar store that has a single 2 1/2 inch opening and it works very well on small jars. I also use it to turn my entrance doorknob, where it works very well. My third choice is the Zyliss 20780 [[ASIN:B002O3Y7I2 Zyliss 20780 Strong Boy Handheld Jar Opener]], which I had to play with for awhile before I figured out the trick to keep it from slipping. Once I managed to solve that problem, it works as well as the Power Grip. Eventually, I'll buy an electric jar opener and give it a test "drive".

I almost forgot the old Gilhoolie twister jar opener [[ASIN:B002VNGBY8 Twister Jar Opener]]which I loved when my hands were good; it's an excellent product that has been around for about a century, varied from the original design, but still great for people without arthritis and perhaps those with mild arthritis. Another good product for people with good hands because it still requires a nice manual grip is the Amco Swing Away [[ASIN:B000HMC5JA Amco Swing-A-Way 711BK Comfort Grip Jar Opener, Black]]. Both the Gilhoolie and the Swing Away are mostly metal.

If you're selecting a jar opener for yourself or with someone with a disability, please keep in mind that there are various levels of disabilities; some people are weaker than others, so the best way to find the right product is to give it a test "drive".

Please Beware!. I received the Oster convection oven as a gift.  It's a beautiful unit, which is why I gave it two stars instead of one.  But I can't permit the aesthetic design to fool me.  Two of the four feet were missing pads and, of greater importance, the clock advanced over 2 minutes per day.  In 8 days, while I pondered the situation, the clock had advanced 22 minutes.  A racing clock on a cooking unit or other performance device is a major problem.  On an oven, we use that digital display to set time and temperature so if it isn't displaying properly, the oven won't have the correct time or temperature.  Because it's racing, you'll end up with under-cooked or unevenly cooked food, which some reviewers have complained about.  In a worse case scenario, the oven could also become a fire hazard.  Either way, I was very worried as well as concerned that the unit had arrived as a lovely and well intention gift.  Nonetheless, I contacted the buyer and Amazon.  Amazon has been great because although they had listed the oven as non-refundable, they have offered to refund the cost.  My friend is presently awaiting that refund and I hope that she gets it.

Filling Boiled Out of Blueberry Mini-Pies, Required Major Cleanup. My husband loves home-made pies, so I thought it would be fun to make mini-pies from time to time, just to change things up a little. After reading the Amazon reviews for various competing mini-pie makers, I ordered this well-reviewed SUNBEAM 4-PIECE PIE MAKER. Little did I know what it had in store for me!

I followed the booklet's recipe for blueberry mini-pies to the letter. I lightly oiled the pie cups, preheated the pie maker, used the provided tool to cut top and bottom crusts from Pillsbury ready-made crusts, prepared the filling, used the provided tool to press the bottom crusts into the pie maker, measured 1/2 cup of filling into each bottom crust, added the top crusts, and clamped the top of the pie maker shut.

The pie maker began emitting steam, which seemed odd. After 10 minutes, the pie crusts were done. However, the pie filling had boiled out onto the pie-maker plates, and a lot of it had spilled down the outside and into the hinges. Because the pie-maker plates were hot, the filling was busily burning onto the plates. As I was removing the mini-pies, the bottom of one burst and dropped all its filling. The final straw was my husband's comment that his intact mini-pie seemed "kind of filled with air"!

Oh well. Maybe I should have used one of the booklet's two recipes for pie crusts--although the booklet did say you could use ready-made crusts from the grocery store. Or maybe I should have crimped the top and bottom crusts together--although the instructions did not say to do this, and the plates look like they will do the crimping when you close the lid.

The cleanup was such a nightmare, I have no desire to ever use this appliance again. The mini-pies are cute, but the preparation time is about the same as for a full-sized, double-crust blueberry pie (except that a 9" pie needs 45 minutes to bake). Also, the mini-pies don't hold much filling, especially if you have to use less than 1/2 cup of filling. I rate this Sunbeam 4-piece pie maker at 2 stars ("I don't like it" on the official Amazon scale).

Good Features Are Far Outweighed by Bad Features. The VORNADO VS-410 ESSENTIAL FABRIC STEAMER comes with a big lint brush, a fabric brush attachment, a travel case, and an 8-foot cord with an attached Velcro strap (for securing the wrapped-up cord). The steamer heats up quickly (in about 2 minutes); it delivers a fairly substantial amount of steam; and it stays cool on the bottom (so it won't burn or set fire to any flat surface you set it on when it's hot).

However, these good features are far outweighed by the many bad features of this product:

*** The steamer is designed only for steaming items that are hanging up--it strongly prefers to be operated in a vertical position. If you want to steam an item laid flat on a bed, and hold the steamer horizontally (like an iron), the steamer spits water droplets even when not overfilled.

*** The water tank capacity is inadequate. On a "max fill", my steamer delivered steam for only 8 minutes (not the promised 10 minutes). Worse, when you open the top to refill the tank, there is still some steam inside, even after the steamer has stopped delivering steam and has gone quiet. (The instructions do say that you should turn the steamer off and let it cool completely before refilling the tank.)

*** The water tank fill window is badly placed. It's difficult to fill the steamer exactly to the "max fill" line, because you can't easily see the window while you're filling the tank at a faucet. Worse, you cannot check the water level when you're actually steaming a garment without aiming the steam directly at your face!

*** The power button is badly placed. Located on the top of the handle, the power button turns off at the slightest touch. My steamer kept turning off when I was simply trying to steam out creases, until I realized that I was hitting the power button as I moved the hand holding the steamer.

*** For a travel steamer, this one is kind of heavy. The steamer and fabric brush attachment alone weigh 1 lb. 11.5 oz.; add the lint brush and travel bag, and the whole thing weighs 1 lb. 15 oz. (almost 2 lbs.).

*** The power does not shut off automatically when the water tank is empty.

*** The 8-foot cord is just barely long enough for a steamer intended to be used on hanging garments.

*** The steamer needs cleaning every 3-6 months with Vornado CleanCycle crystals (two packets supplied with steamer).

My plan was to use this steamer for blocking hand-knit garments, which need to be steamed to give them a finished look. However, it's a really bad choice for knitters! The steam output time is very short, and the steamer doesn't work well in a horizontal position.

My old [[ASIN:B00005OU01 Sunbeam Garment Steamer]] (weighing 1 lb. 5.1 oz. complete with brushes and travel case) is easier to use, and includes the ability to deliver extra steam; it's a better all-around fabric steamer (but apparently discontinued by Sunbeam). This Vornado steamer was a real disappointment, because I'm very happy with my other Vornado products (an oscillating fan, a room air circulator, and a humidifier). I rate this steamer at 2 stars ("I don't like it" on the official Amazon scale).

Approved for One-Handed Use, But Breaks Down Quickly. EDIT: Rating downgraded from 5 stars to 2 stars. Sad to say, this can opener stopped working properly after about six months of light use. The jaws started opening out of sequence, ran even more slowly than before, and would no longer open most jars. Changing the batteries didn't help. The opener had not been dropped or obviously damaged in any way. My husband went back to using his manual [[ASIN:B000079XW2 OXO Good Grips Smooth Edge Can Opener]], which is relatively easy to operate one-handed, and is highly recommended.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
This amazing Hamilton Beach Automatic Jar Opener easily opens jars with 1" to 4" diameter lids. I call it amazing, because you wouldn't expect a device powered by only two AA batteries to have the "grip strength" to open tightly sealed pickle jars! I tested this opener on both large and small pickle jars that always make me use a tool to break the seal, a peanut butter jar, and an extremely hard-to-open prune juice bottle. It worked every time.

All you need to do, is hold the jar steady, place and hold the opener on top of the jar lid, and press the "Open Jar" button. This activates the opener's two sets of gripper arms (which move quite slowly). The first set moves to grasp the jar; then the second set moves in to grip and rotate the lid. When the jar is open, you press the "Release Lid" button. The opener then releases the lid and automatically returns its gripper arms to the proper position for storage and/or the next use.

The instructions say that this jar opener is intended to open only glass jars with metal lids, and NOT intended to open plastic jars. However, it opened my plastic peanut butter jar and plastic prune juice bottle without difficulty. Just keep in mind that you use the opener on plastic jars at your own risk. Perhaps some plastic jars are too fragile to withstand the force applied by the gripper arms and jaws?

My husband, who has full use of only one hand, is able to open jars easily with this gadget. He holds the jars in a vise in a kitchen workstation designed for one-handed cooks (e.g., [[ASIN:B000HZU06C Swedish Cutting Board]]), and operates the opener with his good hand. Because this device is a great help to anyone who even occasionally has difficulty opening jars, I rate it at an unqualified 5 stars.

Cosmetically-Challenged Nightlight/Clock With Awkward Setting Process, Dim Display. This PHILIPS AJH510/37 ALARM CLOCK is a decent night light--with four pretty, easily-changed colors to choose from--but not a particularly good choice for a bedside clock. At the highest brightness setting, the digital time readout is dim, and it's hard to see what time it is in the daytime. The night light (at the bottom of the clock) isn't exactly dim, but it doesn't provide much ambient light for the room--it serves mainly to show the clock's location. Certainly this nightlight/clock will not keep any sleeper awake!

The clock won't win any beauty contests, either. It's a mystery to me, why the manufacturer chose a battleship grey color for the fabric covering. Perhaps to suggest metal mesh? The grey background doesn't help the visibility of the dim orange readout at all. And the grey color doesn't harmonize well with the faux wood plastic disk atop the clock. The photo on the product page is fairly accurate regarding the clock's looks.

The clock's worst feature is the time and alarm-setting process. Depending on what you're trying to do, you must press a button or a location on the faux wood disc, and then fumble around with the volume control wheel to change the hours and minutes, type of alarm (buzzer or nature sounds), display brightness, etc. For me, the task of adjusting hours and minutes up and down, while holding the clock in hand and rolling a sideways-mounted wheel, is extremely awkward. Also, I found the pictorial "quick start" instructions hard to interpret when figuring out the alarm- and feature-setting process. The downloadable manual is similarly pictorial, but is slightly clearer.

At first, I was very confused by the "8UZ" setting, which was how I read the "BUZ" (for buzzer alarm) setting on the display. As for the buzzer alarm itself, it is one of those that starts with a soft beep and increases in volume and frequency until the sleeper wakes and stops it. (I like these.) However, at the very highest volume, the buzzer is probably not loud enough to wake a very sound sleeper.

As for the preloaded nature-sounds (and three music sounds), I listened to them all, but didn't like any except the "train" (railroad boxcars rolling past)--which is only appropriate for go-to-sleep use. (Go-to-sleep is one of the clock's features.) The nature sounds were probably recorded from nature, but they sound artificial. The music sounds include an "angelic harp" that I would quickly tire of, for either wake-up or go-to-sleep purposes.

Because of the ugly-duckling appearance, awkward setting process, and dim clock display, I rate this Philips AJH510/37 Alarm Clock at 2 stars ("I don't like it" on the official Amazon scale).

Scary, Awkward-to-Use Grill Lacks On/Off Switch, Temperature Control. To only make grilled cheese sandwiches and panini, I thought this GEORGE FOREMAN 4-SERVING REMOVABLE PLATE GRILL AND PANINI PRESS (Black, GRP1060B) would be satisfactory for my needs. Wrong, wrong, wrong!

My grill arrived new in the box, and it didn’t smoke or smell bad when I followed the manufacturer’s instructions to start by heating it empty for 15 minutes (to burn off any manufacturing oil or residue). However, the budget-priced (about $29 on Amazon) grill is rather scary to use.

First, there is NO on/off switch or temperature control. The grill heats when you plug it in, and it gets VERY hot in about 5 minutes. You turn the grill off by unplugging it, and it takes quite a while to cool enough for you to remove the dishwasher-safe plates. At least the cord doesn’t heat up, and it doesn’t spark when you unplug it.

Second, the hinge, which “adjusts” to handle thicker or thinner items placed on the grill, is very clunky. When you open the lid and pull up, the hinge pulls up to make a wider space between the two grill plates. However, the hinge doesn’t pull evenly or all that easily.

Third, all of the black plastic parts (including the adjustable hinge) get hot when the grill is heated. You really need to handle this grill with oven mitts or hot pads.

Fourth, the electrical cord is extremely short--shorter than most “short cord” countertop appliances that use a short cord as a safety feature. Because the cord is so short, the cord won’t reach my kitchen countertop outlet unless I place the grill sideways on the countertop. This makes it awkward to load the grill, which is really designed to be opened from the front.

The worst of these four bad features is the lack of a temperature control. The only temperature is “very hot”, so it’s hard to toast grilled cheese sandwiches or panini sandwiches without burning them.

I wouldn’t dream of purchasing this grill for use in cooking meats or grilling vegetables. While the grill isn’t exactly flimsy, it is clear that the manufacturer has put the minimum amount of material into the grill’s manufacture. I’m pretty sure that the grill will burn out or quit working fairy soon if it is used at all regularly.

Only Fits Vacuums With Round Connectors. Before you buy this HOMESOURCE FLEX 'N SEEK CREVICE TOOL, be sure to check the shape of your vacuum's connectors. Thus it only fits one of my three Bissell vacuums. The adapter adjusts for larger or smaller round connectors, but not for square connectors.

The crevice tool will fit into or under 1/2" wide spaces. It won't fit under my refrigerator, as I'd hoped (though that was probably an unrealistic hope). More significantly, the flexible tip isn't very flexible. The tool is bent into a curved shape by the packaging, and I'm going to have to place weights on it to straighten it out. Out of the box, it's hard to use, because the stiff curve makes it difficult to maneuver into tight spaces, and to keep the tool end flat against the floor for good suction.

Because this intriguing tool is poorly designed, and doesn't fit vacuums with square connectors, I rate it at 2 stars ("I don't like it" on the official Amazon scale).

Fabulous Looks, But Overall Poor Design. This MR.COFFEE 12-CUP PROGRAMMABLE COFFEEMAKER, STAINLESS STEEL looks fabulous, brews fast, has easy-to-use buttons, includes a water filtration system, has a keep-warm plate, and includes a cleaning cycle setting. Unfortunately, the coffeemaker also has a hard-to-fill reservoir, a clumsy "removable filter basket", and an exposed showerhead-type water system that emits steam when the lid is opened.

The good looks are not enough to make me like this coffeemaker! Everything (coffee grounds and water) must be added from the top. This is all right when the coffeemaker is cold. However, if you open the top to add coffee for a second pot right after the first pot has brewed, the showerhead will send a cloud of steam straight into your face. (I strongly prefer a coffeemaker with an enclosed showerhead and a coffee basket that swings out sideways, like the slower-brewing [[ASIN:B0041A5H5S Hamilton Beach 12-Cup Digital Coffee Maker]].)

The lid on this Mr. Coffee coffeemaker has a second lid in the back half that flips up. I think this is intended for you to use in filling the reservoir, but the second lid doesn't always want to stay up. It's also faster to fill the reservoir by opening the entire lid. When you open the top, the entire mechanism with the showerhead feels flimsy, as if it will break easily (and early breakage has been my experience with this type of coffeemaker design).

The outer "removable filter basket" lacks a handle for easy removal. It has ear-like tabs that are hard to grip (especially if the coffeemaker is hot) and require using two hands to pull the basket up and out. If you're using the water filtration system, you will probably want to remove this outer basket for every pot, because you must put ground coffee (inside a paper or permanent filter) into the basket, and then place the water filtration system over the top of the basket. The water filtration system itself consists of a charcoal filter disk that slides into a frame or lid for the "removable filter basket".

The water filtration system is supposed to remove chlorine from your water, to make your coffee taste better. You need to change the charcoal filter every month. (The coffeemaker comes with just one filter.) This isn't very useful to me, because my tap water often tastes odd because of organic matter. Removing chlorine isn't enough, so I filter my coffee water with a different type of filter before adding it to the coffeemaker's water reservoir.

My coffeemaker arrived without either paper filters or the "Mr. Coffee nylon permanent filter" that is supposed to be included (according to the instructions). I guess that the permanent filter got removed in the warehouse, because the box wasn't completely sealed when it arrived. Some kind of additional filter is needed inside the "removable filter basket", or coffee grounds will escape into the carafe during brewing.

The coffeemaker comes with a short 26" cord, which is more or less standard for kitchen appliances now, especially heating appliances. The cord arrives coiled inside the coffeemaker's base, and needs to be pulled out when you first set up the coffeemaker.

Because of the many bad design features, I rate it this Mr. Coffee coffeemaker (Model BVMC-JPX37-AM) at 2 stars ("I don't like it" on the official Amazon scale).

Serving Rack Must Be Placed on Heat Mat; Stone Should Be Cleaned With Metal Scraper. This JAMIE OLIVER PIZZA STONE AND SERVING RACK (round earthenware stone,14 inch) consists of a thin, lightweight stone that fits into a simple chrome-plated wire rack.

The rack is rather useless, because it only raises the stone about 3/8” from the surface it rests on, and requires hotpads or a heat mat underneath to protect that surface. (It's also questionable whether you’d want to serve a pizza at table on the stone taken directly from the oven, because the stone gets really HOT!)

The weight of the stone--very light for earthenware--is a plus. The 14” size is perfect for baking an 11” frozen pizza and getting a crispy crust. (My pizza was a frozen Newman’s Own Four-Cheese Pizza.)

However, the stone’s cleaning instructions add up to a huge minus. To wit: “It is best to scrape food residue off your stone with a metal spatula after the stone has cooled. It is recommended not to use water to clean your stone as this may leave moisture in the pores of the stone that may cause the stone to crack when heated in the oven.” The directions go on to say that if you must use water, you should use ONLY plain water (no detergent), and allow the stone to dry thoroughly before using it again.

The instructions also note that the “pizza stone will acquire stains through use”. That's absolutely true. After one use, my stone has burned-on residue and oil stains that make it unattractive for serving anything at all. (The stone is still perfectly functional for high-temperature baking, of course.) This product was a disappointment, because I wanted it for serving (with the rack).

Quieter, More Compact Than Cuisinart; But Cuisinart Has More Advantages. I wondered whether this TRIPLE SCOOP 1.5 QUART ICE CREAM MAKER (TS-562-Red; about $59 on Amazon) would be an improvement over my much-used [[ASIN:B003KYSLMW Cuisinart 1.5 Quart Ice Cream Maker]] (about $48 on Amazon). The answer is "Yes and No", but mostly "No".

+++Yes, the Triple Scoop is quieter (a lot quieter); it takes up less storage space (freezer tub and motorized lid only; no separate motor base and big plastic cover); and it freezes the ice cream slightly harder (at least when you use the Triple Scoop ice cream mix (one vanilla, one strawberry, one chocolate packet included).

+++No, the Triple Scoop has a too-small, too-narrow spout for adding ice cream mix (the mix spills unless you're very careful or you use a funnel); the finished ice cream is difficult to remove from the paddle (most of the ice cream comes out with the paddle, too); the Triple Scoop motor element is difficult to remove from the clear plastic lid for cleaning (the motor element plus lid is also hard to grip when you're attaching it to the freezer tub); the Triple Scoop has no recipes for making ice cream from scratch with your own ingredients (the instructions say to buy the Triple Scoop ice cream mix packages).

The two machines make about the same quantity of "soft-serve" ice cream (put it in the freezer if you want more solidly frozen ice cream). Both machines use freezer tubs that must be placed in a freezer for 24 hours for best results. (Note that if your ice cream isn't freezing, you can't just run the machine longer than the recommended 20 minutes or so, because the tubs warm up during use.) The freezer tubs are hand-washable only (because they contain something liquid that freezes hard in the freezer). None of the Triple Scoop parts are dishwasher safe; some of the Cuisinart parts are dishwasher safe.

The notion that you need to purchase Triple Scoop ice cream mix to make homemade ice cream is kind of ridiculous. All you need for ice cream is 2 cups of milk, half-and-half, or heavy cream, plus some sugar and flavorings. You can use recipes from anywhere, as long as you don't overload the motor by adding two many extra ingredients like chopped fruit or nuts. I tried the included Triple Scoop Strawberry ice cream mix, and didn't care for it. It tasted like strawberries, but also faintly like artificial flavoring and preservatives (so it's not for anyone who wants to avoid the chemical additives in commercial ice cream).

Overall, I much prefer my very noisy, storage-space-hogging, Cuisinart ice cream maker (shown with a purple tub from an all-purple model).

Impressive Features But Performs Poorly--Has Inadequate Battery, Suction; Needs Supervision. Compared to my [[ASIN:B008LX6OC6 Roomba 650]] (plus [[ASIN:B019OH9898 Braava Jet]]), this ECOVACS DEEBOT M88 ROBOTIC VACUUM CLEANER, DRY AND WET MOP FEATURE WITH SMARTPHONE CONTROL (White) just doesn't cut it. The robot’s Achilles’ heel is the inadequate battery--a full 4-hour charge gives you about 45 minutes, which is NOT enough to finish vacuuming a small, carpeted living room with obstacles (furniture, clutter). Recharging, to complete the job, takes hours.

Standard suction is also inadequate. The robot does NOT pick up larger dirt particles, rice grains, or other gritty bits. To keep a carpet or even a bare floor clean, regular vacuuming with an upright or canister vacuum will still be required. The robot runs slowly, and the random pattern (required for carpet) changes directions so often, it is impossible to get full floor coverage in a single run.

Cleaning the dirt collecter is very complicated--you must open the top, pull up a handle to remove the dirt bin, open a gate to empty the dirt and dust bunnies, and then clean off a thin sponge that protects a high-efficiency filter. (I had to retrieve the sponge from the trash, after I inadvertently dumped it along with the collected dirt.) Then you have to reverse the steps to replace the bin.

The robot requires quite a bit of supervision when working. It has a sloped top edge that causes it to get stuck easily under low furniture or obstacles. It does NOT climb over flat area rugs, or easily move from bare floor to carpet. (The instructions say you should use physical barriers, and vacuum carpeted and bare floors separately.) The sensors could be a lot better--the robot spends a lot of time thinking about what to do after meeting an obstacle, and it isn't very good at detecting stairsteps or “cliffs”.

When the battery needs recharging, the robot slows to a pathetic crawl. It may not have enough power left to find its way back to the recharging station. Placing the robot on the charger by hand is fiddly, and the robot is easily jarred off the charger contacts. The robot has an inconveniently placed on/off switch underneath--and you have to turn the robot off if you want it to hold a charge away from the charger.

The robot has three cleaning patterns--random, back and forth, and around the edges of the room. The default pattern is random, and you must use the remote (included) or the app to change the pattern. My remote changed the robot to the “edge” pattern, but would NOT change the pattern to “back and forth” (the pattern recommended for bare floors, that I really needed for cleaning under a queen-sized bed).

When it comes to wet-mopping, this robot is too large to mop my bathrooms. It can't get into the small spaces alongside the toilets, and the round shape means it can't mop close to the room edges or under the cabinet overhangs.

In sum, this Eurovac robot is unsuitable for regularly cleaning rooms that have a fair amount of furniture or clutter, or for wet mopping rooms with tight spaces. Because my iRobot devices do both tasks easily, I think that this Eurovac device is very expensive (about $450 on Amazon) for what it is. I wanted a second robot vacuum for convenience in cleaning the upstairs, and was impressed by all of this robot’s advertised features (especially the included remote), but I’m very, very disappointed by the Eurovac robot’s actual performance.

Toasts Unevenly, Barely Toasts on Highest Setting. After my much-loved Hamilton Beach Digital 4-Slice Toaster developed a short (after long use), I purchased this HAMILTON BEACH 4-SLICE EXTRA WIDE SLOT TOASTER (with Defrost and Bagel Functions, Shade Selector, Toast Boost, Auto-Shutoff and Cancel Button, Black (24633)) as a replacement. What a disappointment!

It’s hard to select the toasting time, because the printed shade selector numbers and pointer are small and faint. Frozen bread barely toasts when the shade selector is set to 6 or the maximum 7. The toaster toasts the bread unevenly (only the top half), and mostly toasts only on one side. When I toasted English muffins, one muffin failed to pop up at the end of the cycle, even though the muffin went in smoothly.

The crumb trays, which should be emptied weekly, are inconveniently placed. To empty them, you must unplug the toaster and turn it upside down over a sink or garbage receptacle.

Because I’ve owned many excellent Hamilton Beach toasters in the past, I have to wonder whether this particular toaster model is a counterfeit knockoff. The design flaws I can live with, but the performance is barely there when the toaster is brand new.

Looks Good, But Too Dull to Make Zest or Curls. This SAVORA STAINLESS STEEL BAR ZESTER looks fabulous, but it's so dull, it won't produce either zest or curls from a thick-skinned supermarket lemon (see, e.g., [[ASIN:B008NW0GHO Tropicana Premium Fresh Lemons]]). To even attempt to use it--applying considerable force--you need to turn it upside down (Savora label underneath) to get the "sharp" edges turned toward the lemon skin.

If you need a zester, OXO makes a very good one that actually does the things that this one claims to do (see [[ASIN:B00004OCJO B00004OCJO Good Grips Lemon Zester]]).

Ugly Bedside Organizer Needs 11" Clearance From Mattress to Floor. This INTERDESIGN 04953 WREN BEDSIDE STORAGE ORGANIZER (for Phone, Tablet, Magazines, Water Bottle, Remote Control - 4 Pockets, Light Gray) is just plain ugly. It's made of heavy, coarse, taupe canvas that is stitched (and probably glued) to a stiff, rubberized ivory backing. The fabric feels unpleasant to the touch.

The organizer doesn't hold thick items, because the large and medium pockets are stitched down almost flat to the backing. Only the water bottle pocket has gussets to allow for insertion of a bulky item. The product photo showing the pockets curving outward is misleading. That mostly happens when items are inserted into the pockets, and then the organizer doesn't lie flat against the side of the bed.

The organizer installs easily by pushing the wire frame between the mattress and box springs, but it hangs almost to the floor on my bed. (It needs 11" vertical clearance from the bottom of the mattress to the floor.) As a result, the organizer is in the way of my feet when I get into bed, if I install it where it's easiest to reach when I'm in bed.

The between-the-mattress-and-box-springs installation means that the organizer (with its contents) must be removed whenever you change the sheets. The organizer also gets in the way of your bedcovers, unless you install it at the very head of the bed. The organizer can be easily removed from the wire frame for cleaning, because it is attached with a strip of heavy Velcro.

I was hoping to use this organizer to hold things that wouldn't fit on my crowded bedside table, but it's too inconvenient for regular use. InterDesign products are usually much nicer than this one.

Moderate Suction, Easily Clogged Motor Filter. This budget-priced (about $40 on Amazon) DIRT DEVIL POWER EXPRESS LITE PET 3-IN-1 CORDED STICK VACUUM (SD22020B) has only moderate suction, and doesn't “pick up” well on carpeted floors, even though it has a powered brush.

When I tried it on carpeted stairs, the motor filters became clogged with fine fuzz almost immediately, and the vac began dropping fuzz back on the carpet. (The troubleshooting guide says this will happen if the motor filter is clogged.) The filter is easy to remove and clean (by brushing it off), but it's very small, without much capacity for fine dust or lint.

I can't imagine using this vac for a large carpeted area. My household has no pets, the stairs are vacuumed fairly often, and the vac picked up only a small amount of hair--yet the filter needed cleaning after only a few minutes of operation. The larger dirt cannister is extremely easy to remove and empty, but it collected almost nothing from my carpeted stairs.

I wanted this vac to clean areas that my Roomba 650 cannot reach, and I suppose it will work for that. However, I was disappointed in this model, because Dirt Devil is a brand that I have come to trust. A Dirt Devil detailer, a Dirt Devil hand vac, and a Dirt Devil upright vac have all performed very well for me in the past.

Cleans Pod Capsule Only; Does Not Eliminate Need for Descaling. These KEURIG 5000057588 K-CUP COFFEE MAKER RINSE PODS (10 Count, White) only clean your coffee maker’s pod capsule—they are NOT a substitute for regular descaling of your entire coffee maker (see [[ASIN:B00FOT9W5Q Keurig Descaling Solution]]). The rinse pods cleanse the pod area (where you place the pods) and the channel below, to prevent “flavour carryover” between brews—especially between cups of hot chocolate, apple cider, or fancy flavored coffees and cups of plain coffee or tea.

To use the rinse pods, you need to (1) insert a rinse pod and brew a cup with water; (2) remove the used rinse pod and discard the rinse water; (3) rinse the pod capsule by brewing another cup with water only; and (4) discard the rinse water. In practice, I needed to rinse the pod capsule twice, because the first rinse produced a cup of hot rinse water with a white ring of chemicals around the water surface.

I think it’s easier to rinse the pod capsule (to reduce flavour carryover) by brewing one cup of plain water and discarding the rinse water. Doing it that way also avoids adding mildly toxic chemicals to your coffee maker.

The rinse pods contain maltodextrin, sodium bicarbonate, citric acid, and sodium citrate. The warning on the box says “do not consume”; and, among other things, advises you to “Seek medical attention if a large amount is swallowed, if irritation persists, or if you feel unwell.”

Mesmerizingly Beautiful When Lit, But Design of Base Is Faulty. This HIMALAYAN SALT COMPANY PILLAR LAMP is mesmerizingly beautiful when turned on. However, it is totally different from what I expected. The lamp iS NOT a solid pillar of salt inside an ironwork base; instead it's a collection of loose lumps of salt inside an ironwork basket that is shaped like a pillar.

When the lamp arrived, the salt lumps were contained in a plastic bag inside the basket. The bag had to be removed before the lamp could be used; the same was true of cardboard central core that protected the little 15-watt bulb (at the bottom of the basket) from breakage during shipping. The only way to remove the bag was to carefully dump out the salt chunks. Fortunately they were easy to replace, though they left a pile of loose salt behind.

The salt chunks were okay with me, but then I discovered that the lamp would NOT stand up straight. The reason was that the connection between the light bulb and the electrical cord was contacting the countertop beneath the lamp. That connection was longer than the three little ball-shaped legs--so the electrical cord connection was taking the place of one leg, and tilting the whole lamp to one side.

I’m NOT comfortable, sleeping or working next to an electric lamp with such a poorly designed base. This is all the more true because the lamp is supposed to be turned on for long hours to get the promised therapeutic effect.

If I’d looked closely at the product page photo before ordering, I’d have realized the salt came in chunks; and I have to admit that the chunks probably add to the lamp’s beauty when it's lighted up. However, there is no easy fix possible for the “fourth leg” on the black basket-shaped base, and I don't trust the safety of this electric lamp.

Small, Base Metal Tins Belong in Dollar Store. These MIND READER METAL CANISTERS (3 Piece, Galvanized Metal, Silver) are vastly overpriced (about $21 on Amazon). They are lightweight, base metal tins with loose-fitting lids. (A rubber gasket helps seal the lids, but you can’t even lift an empty tin by the lid handle.)

The advertised 6-cup capacity is too little to hold much of anything, unless you want the tins for an employee break room to hold sugar packets, individually-wrapped tea bags, and K-cups or instant coffee packets. The tins aren’t good for holding other things (e.g., home-baked cookies, hard candies), because of the labels for “Coffee”, “Sugar”, and “Tea”. Whatever you put in these, it will need frequent replenishment because of the tins’ small size.

Overall, the tins look and feel cheap. The silver finish has an odd, tacky feel, even when the tins are brand new. The gold-toned metal labels are hard to read and marginally attractive—yet they are probably the reason for the inflated price. This set is something that I would expect to find in a Dollar Store.

There are no included “use and care” instructions, so I’m guessing that they are “wipe clean” only. Dishwasher detergent will probably leave pits in the surface.

Square Candle Holders Are Too Small for U.S. Votive Candles, Tea Lights. These ROYAL IMPORTS GLASS VOTIVE CANDLE HOLDERS (European Style, Set of 6, Unfilled) are pretty--I love the square shape--but they’re too small for standard U.S. tea lights or votive candles. The standard candles simply don’t fit.

You can burn standard candles in the square holders, but the metal bases of the candles are wider than the interiors of the holders (at the bottom). Thus the candles stop about ¼” short of settling all the way into the holders, and the candles must be positioned carefully if you want them to be level.

Beautiful Electric Water Kettle. This SECURA SWK-1701DB STAINLESS STEEL DOUBLE WALL ELECTRIC WATER KETTLE (1.8 Quart, Black Onyx) is beautiful. However, the electrical cord gets too warm for me to feel comfortable using it. The fact that it rusts in places is also a big deal-killer.

With electric heating appliances, I prefer to stick with “name brands” like Hamilton Beach, General Electric, or Black and Decker. I know that these companies manufacture their products in China, but I feel that they do a pretty good job with quality control and design. Thus I’m not worried about the products' becoming electrical hazards.

This “Secura” brand electric water kettle was a very poor buying choice for me.

Slow to Grind Enough Beans for 12-Cup Drip Coffee Maker. This SECURA AUTOMATIC COFFEE GRINDER AND SPICE GRINDER (2.5 Ounce Capacity, Silver) works on the same principle as my tried-and-true KitchenAid coffee grinder. (That grinder has been grinding away for over 20 years--I don’t know why KitchenAid stopped making this great appliance.) Basically, you put your beans or seeds into the bladed stainless steel bowl, add the plastic lid, add the square plastic cover, and press down on the square cover in 8-second bursts to grind the stuff in the bowl.

An 8-second burst grinds 2 tablespoons of coffee beans to the equivalent of a “percolator” grind. This is too coarse a grind for my Hamilton Beach Coffeemaker, so my beans need additional 8-second bursts. Given that my ancient KitchenAid appliance grinds 8 tablespoons of coffee beans to the equivalent of a “drip” grind in just 10 seconds, the Secura grinder won’t be replacing it.

Another reason NOT to embrace the Secura grinder is that the bladed bowl doesn’t hold enough coffee beans at one time for 10-12 cups of coffee. The “Max Fill” line only accommodates the beans for about 6 cups of coffee. For 12 cups of coffee, you have to fill the bladed bowl twice, and grind each time in at least two 8-second bursts. If you don’t grind in short bursts, the grinder will overheat and shut down--and require a 45-minute cooldown.

Finally, the plastic lid that goes onto the bladed stainless steel bowl fits very tightly. It is quite difficult to remove. This is a major drawback when you’re opening a container of finely ground coffee beans or seeds.

The grinder bowl, plastic lid, and square plastic cover are all dishwasher safe, but hand washing is recommended. A reason to follow this recommendation is that plastic becomes cloudy if it’s subjected to high dishwasher temperatures.

I can use this grinder for spices, but I don’t grind a lot of spices, except for nutmeg. For nutmeg, I use a specialized nutmeg grinder that looks like a peppermill, so that the nutmeg is always freshly ground.

Very Poor Smooth-Edge Can Opener—Requires Far Too Much Hand Strength. Once you’ve tried a good “lid-lifter” can opener, you won’t want to use a “lid-cutter” can opener ever again. The “smooth edge” lid-lifters pull the entire lid off the can—the lid is held on with adhesive—leaving no sharp edges around the lid to cut you when the can is opened. Unfortunately, this SWING-A-WAY SMOOTH EDGE CAN OPENER (522448; 7.5”, Black) is NOT one of the good ones. It requires far too much hand strength to twist the knob and propel the opener around the can.

This is actually the first Swing-a-Way opener that I haven’t liked, and I’m really surprised that it’s so hard to use. Two very good lid-lifter openers are the battery-operated [[ASIN:B00QHPOHSS Bartelli Soft Edge Can Opener]], and the manual [[ASIN:B000079XW2 OXO Smooth Edge Can Opener]]. My stroke-disabled husband (who is one-handed but still cooks) uses the Bartelli opener every day, because it opens cans reliably, without the need to twist any knobs.

This Swing-a-Way smooth edge opener might be a good substitute for one of those hand-squeeze devices that athletes use to strengthen their hand grip.

Beige Rubber “Feet” Spoil Elegant Look. This ZONESUM CERAMIC, MODERN, ELEGANT FLOWER VASE (8.75" Tall, 4.5" Opening, Silver) looks okay from a distance, but rather cheap up close. The beige rubber anti-slip “feet” really spoil the elegant look. The feet don’t match the black, gray, and silver exterior; they are visible when the vase stands on a flat surface; and they are placed unevenly so that they extend beyond the base.

The vase has a narrow opening, about 2’ wide and 4.5” long, so it is a bit of a challenge to arrange flowers in it. I don’t think that the opening is wide enough to accept any kind of frog to hold the flower stems.

To make a really nice flower arrangement, you need to start by replacing the beige rubber feet with black ones, or with green table-protector fabric.

Medium-Sized-Room Humidifier Has All Desirable Features. UPDATE 3/12/18: After several months of uneventful operation, my humidifier began intermittently leaking badly onto the floor. I finally figured out that the water reservoir in the base, which hydrates the wick, was overfilling. This was happening because the valve on the refillable water tank, which controls the automatic delivery of water as needed during operation, was malfunctioning. This was NOT user error. It is a basic design or manufacturing flaw. Rating changed from 5 stars to 1 star.

This VORNADO ENERGY SMART EVAPORATIVE HUMIDIFIER (EVDC300, with Automatic Shut-off, 1 Gallon Capacity, LED Display) has all the features that I want in a medium-room-size humidifier. First, when it's running in the “Energy Smart” mode (indicated by a green light next to the lighted power button), it turns off automatically when it runs out of water.

Second, it remembers the settings when it's turned off. After you power it off and on again while refilling the tank, you don't have to punch all the buttons again for (1) humidity level, (2) fan speed, and (3) automatic, continuous, or Energy Smart mode.

Third, it has a 1-gallon tank that lasts about 30 hours (when I keep it in Energy Smart mode, on high fan speed, with 60% humidity). The tank is easy to refill, because it has a wide circular top opening, and isn't too heavy when filled with water. The tank has a built-in handle that makes it easy to carry.

Fourth, it has a single wick (a mesh sheet that soaks up water from the tank). This needs to be replaced when it gets hard enough that it won’t wick up water, or when it develops algae or mold. The wick contains an antimicrobial additive, and you can extend the wick’s life by adding a bacteriostatic solution that suppresses algae growth to the water tank. The wick is supposed to last 4-8 weeks; using the algae suppressant, my wicks last at least 12 weeks (in Energy Smart mode). (This model uses [[ASIN:B01J664VSA Vornado EVDC300 wicks (2-pack)]].)

Fifth, the fan turns off when the humidifier sensor determines that the set humidity level has been reached. You can set the humidity at anything from 40 to 60 percent (in 5-point steps). The sensor is an approximation, of course--when my humidifier reads 60%, two other nearby sensors read 46% and 56%. It takes a few days for the room humidity to reach the desired level. (The fan can be manually set to run continuously at extra-high speed, if you want to raise the humidity level fast. If you do this, check the water tank frequently, because with this setting the humidifier won't turn off automatically when it’s out of water.)

Finally, the humidifier has a water tank light that pulses a warning when the water level is low.

Great “Hold” Feature, But Falls Short on “Instant Read”. This BEYOND GROUP 1 33 DIGITAL INSTANT READ THERMOCOUPLE THERMOMETER (with Folding Probe) has one great feature--a “Hold” button that locks the reading so you can read it after you remove the probe. However, it is NOT an “instant read” thermometer--when your fingers heat the probe a little by unfolding it, the display is very slow to return to a room temperature reading. Also, It takes many seconds to reach a stable reading after the probe is inserted into hot food.

The thermometer gives readings that are a couple of degrees higher than my expensive [[ASIN:B01M6V1SXE Thermapen]] (which does give instant readings). You’ll want to test this thermometer in boiling water, to determine what the degree readings really mean, if you’re planning to use it to test cooked meats for safety.

The default display shows Centigrade numbers; if you want Fahrenheit, you must press the “Hold” button for 3 seconds. You must reset to Fahrenheit frequently--whenever you power on the thermometer, and whenever it shuts off automatically (after a fairly short time).

The “Hold” button works as promised. When the temperature is locked, the display shows the last reading. (The display blinks when it’s reading temperatures.) However, the “Hold” feature isn’t enough to overcome the thermometer’s other deficiencies.

Great Nonstick Finish, But NOT Dishwasher Safe; Pans Rust. These CASAWARE 9 x 6 x 0.75-INCH TOASTER OVEN BAKING PANS (Silver Granite) are the perfect size for my excellent [[ASIN:B003Z34OME Oster Toaster Oven]], and they have a wonderful nonstick ceramic finish. Cooked food spills slide right off the sheets under running water.

However, the pans are NOT dishwasher safe. I put mine through the dishwasher anyway, expecting some damage to the nonstick finish over time. To my surprise, the finish holds up well, but the pans themselves rust. Water gets into the rolled edges of the pans, and then they drip rusty water onto my clean dishes as I take them out of the dishwasher.

The pans will rust even if you handwash them, as recommended by the manufacturer. For me, the pans are a total loss--and a surprising loss, given how much these pans cost compared to other toaster oven pans.

Worked Great for Nine Months, Then Burned Out. This NINJA 12-CUP PROGRAMMABLE COFFEE MAKER (with Classic and Rich Brews, 60 oz. Water Reservoir, and Thermal Flavor Extraction (CE201), Black/Stainless Steel) made excellent coffee for me for about 9 months. My household drinks a lot of coffee, so the coffee maker was used for an average of two pots per day.

Today, I made a second pot and left the carafe on the warming plate as usual. An hour or so later, the coffee maker began softly beeping. It seemed to have spontaneously attempted to brew another pot of coffee--but of course the water reservoir was empty.

The pot smelled hot, like something was wrong with the electrical parts. I tried turning the coffee maker off and on, but the beeping persisted. Ditto after I unplugged the coffee maker and turned it on again.

Obviously the coffee maker is now unsafe to use, even if the beeping stops after the coffee maker cools down. There is nothing in the instruction booklet about this steady, soft beeping warning. I’m glad that the beeping alerted me to a problem, but I wonder what would have happened if I hadn’t been home when it started up.

Unfortunately, I liked this coffee maker so much, I purchased a backup. I still plan to use the backup, but I will be afraid to leave it plugged in or turned on when I’m not close by. This is an issue, because unplugging the coffee maker cancels the programming, and turning it off cancels the stay warm feature.

I will NOT be purchasing another of these expensive coffee makers. Because the pot was so heavily used, I can accept a 9-month lifespan. But all of my other coffee makers have simply stopped working when they were worn out. This one was burning out, with some kind of electrical malfunction.

Fails as Decorative Piece; Made of Heavy Fake Marble. This INTERDESIGN DAKOTA RESIN MARBLE CENTER (for Toothbrush, Cell Phone; White) is very heavy--it’s almost heavy enough to be marble, but I think it is actually some kind of “cultured stone”. The item has marbling, but doesn’t really look like natural marble.

To my mind, this item fails as a decorative piece. It’s small and blocky, and the metal crosspieces make it look odd. There isn’t any real design to it. Usually InterDesign products are much more attractive than this.

The most interesting feature may be the water drainage hole in the bottom of the toothbrush section. The hole is securely closed with a flexible plastic stopper.

Extremely Dull Cheese Slicer. This AMAZONCOMMERCIAL STAINLESS STEEL CHEESE SLICER was a huge disappointment. It’s very dull--too dull to use to clean mold off the outsides of blocks of cheese. (I picked up the tip about using a cheese slicer to clean up slightly moldy cheese when I attended a wine & cheese tasting event in California’s Wine Country.)

When I tested the slicer on a hardened piece of cheddar cheese (about 2” x 4”), the slicer produced extremely thin slices about 1½” long, no matter how much pressure I applied. My existing cheese slicer produced ¼” thick slices that were a full 4” long.

This is supposedly a “commercial” product. I would hate to be an employee who is expected to use this dull cheese slicer on a regular basis.

The slicer is made of stainless steel. It's dishwasher safe. It has a comfortable-to-hold handle.

More or Less Smokeless, But Many Things NOT to Like. This PHILIPS SMOKE-LESS GRILL (plus Bonus Cleaning Tool, HD6371/98) is very expensive (about $280 on Amazon) for what it is. It cooks with two banks of infrared lights, but that’s NOT why it’s “smokeless”.

It’s smokeless, more or less, because the drip tray is located well below the grill surface, and below the heat sources, so that grease drippings don’t burn hard onto the drip pan (causing smoke). If you’ve ever broiled a steak in an electric oven, you know that most of the smoke comes from grease that is burning onto the broiler pan surface nearest the broiler coils. Thus, with this grill, you’ll still get some smoke if you cook fatty foods.

My appliance didn’t melt at the sides with first use, but there are a lot of things to NOT like about this appliance. First, the handles on the barbecue grid (the loose tray on top) get very hot at the four points where the metal joins the plastic handle insulation. Surprise for the unwary cook!

Second, although there’s a warning against staring at the infrared lights, it’s impossible NOT to look at them, because they’re located right below the barbecue grid. You have to look down on them when you turn the food or check for doneness.

Third, the grill takes 6-7 minutes to preheat, and it sends a lot of heat into your kitchen. You definitely don’t want to use the appliance underneath your kitchen cabinets (danger of setting them on fire). My electric stove’s broiler doesn’t heat the kitchen as much. The appliance also takes quite a while to cool down so that it can be safely cleaned.

Fourth, the appliance is big and awkward to handle. It takes up a lot of countertop or table space.

Fifth, the drip tray slides out from the left end, so it needs a lot of space for removal.

Sixth, the appliance isn’t easy to clean, except for the barbecue grid and the drip tray (both are dishwasher safe). Grease spatters on the insides of the appliance, and must be scraped off. Otherwise, the grease will burn on and start to produce smoke.

Finally, the scraper tool is just a paint scraper with double-edged razor blades (you get three blades). These are readily available at hardware stores.

I’m still scratching my head at the price. I wanted this because my electric oven’s broiler produces some smoke, and because it burns grease onto the broiler pan so badly that I have to clean the pan with Easy-Off. But the broiler and broiler pan are much easier (and safer) to use and to clean than this grilling appliance.

1100-Watt Microwave Burned Popcorn, Scorched Popper in 90 Seconds. After only 90 seconds, the popcorn was burned, and the silicone popper was scorched near the bottom, both inside and outside. (See photos.) Since the instructions suggest heating the popper for 2-4 minutes, the popper seems like a potential fire hazard.

The popcorn did pop. Experimentation with lower cook power and even shorter cooking times may produce edible popcorn. However, it’s not worth the trouble, as the single serving is only about 1½ cups of popcorn.

Also, there’s some waste of dishwashing liquid when you use the soap dispensing holder. You have to fill the lower reservoir with dishwashing liquid, and because this is a pump dispenser, some of the liquid will always be left behind.

The soap reservoir can't be cleaned easily, because it is welded to the white part that contains the pump mechanism. (You can clean the reservoir by filling it full of water instead of soap, but the reservoir is hard to empty.)

Of course, the holder dispenses a measured amount of dishwashing liquid. You may save on dishwashing liquid if you, or someone in your household, always tends to squirt too much liquid from the bottle.

Does NOT Fit Instant Pot Liner, Cuisinart Saucepan. Not My Idea of a "Tad", "Dash", "Pinch", or "Smidgen". These stainless steel NORPRO MINI MEASURING SPOONS will make a cute joke gift for a serious cook, but they're not really useful as measuring spoons (tad, dash, pinch, smidgen, drop), because the measures are overly generous. If you use them with old recipes that call for these amounts, you'll probably overseason your dishes.

My mother taught me that in old recipes, a "tad" is a small amount; a "dash" is one shake from a shaker (e.g., a pepper or salt shaker); a "pinch" is the amount you can pinch between your finger and thumb; a "smidgen" is a very tiny amount (just enough to achieve the right taste); and a "drop" is one drop of liquid (e.g., a drop from a food coloring bottle). Of course these are only approximations, but they're used primarily to mean "cautiously season to taste".

In this set, a "tad" is a scant 1/4 teaspoon; a "dash" is a scant 1/8 teaspoon; a "pinch" is 1/16 teaspoon; a "smidgen" is 1/32 teaspoon; and a "drop" is a generous single drop of food coloring liquid. To me, 1/4 teaspoon is way more than a "tad", and 1/8 teaspoon is much more than a "dash". My idea of a "pinch" matches up with Norpro's idea of a "smidgen".

In sum, these are NOT the really small measuring spoons that I expected (spoons that would measure amounts of 1/8 teaspoon or less). They are well made, of solid stainless steel, and they are dishwasher safe. However, because they measure overly large amounts, I rate them at 2 stars ("I don't like them" on the official Amazon scale).

Charcoal Filter Doesn’t Adequately Seal Off Holes in Stainless Steel Lid. This UTOPIA KITCHEN STAINLESS STEEL COMPOST BIN (for Kitchen Countertop;1.3 Gallon with Lid, Charcoal Filter, 1 Spare Charcoal Filter) is ideally sized for an indoor compost bin, and it has a tight-fitting lid. However, the lid has large holes in it, and the charcoal filter inside the lid is see-through thin.

Thus the bin is a poor choice for my household, because we are constantly battling the ants that have colonized large portions of the Northern California coast. The thin filter may contain odors--or may not--but it doesn’t present an adequate barrier to ants that are attracted by food scrap odors.

When the bin is lined with a compostable bag, the lid fits too snugly, and is hard to remove. The charcoal filter is somewhat hard to pull out and replace, despite the seller's instructions to keep it free of food residue and to sun dry it weekly to avoid microbial growth.

I like the pail handle, and the bin size, and the all-stainless-steel construction. However, this bin won’t work for me, because I want the bin to hold food scraps indoors overnight for later transfer to a big outdoor compost cart.

Possible safety hazard otherwise love it. See VIDEO. [[VIDEOID:add165a37251916141d7ce73c55913b5]] I don't hate it. I will describe why I like it, then why I am giving it just 1 star.

Why I wanted it: We don't do much cooking in the microwave. We had a big microwave taking up precious counter real estate. We didn't want to out right get rid of it since we used it just enough to warrant keeping it. On occasion we use it to reheat something or when I don't feel like using the rice cooker, I will make it in the microwave instead. So my husband looked for a smaller microwave, and selected this one.

Dimensions are as described. As with any product, read the description and compare it to your needs and space. Rounded in the back, narrow width, tall height; more so than most microwaves. It fit snug under my kitchen cabinets. Pushed back into a corner, it freed up much desired space.

We use a lot of Corelle ware products. Fits their very large dinner plates,their regular sized dinner plates, 2 quart bowls, 1 quart bowls. Any other brand of plates have fit in there as well. No problem. Keep your item within the space of the rotating plate and you will be fine. There is no space outside of the rotating plate, so squares or rectangles may not advance.
Fits bags for steam vegetables, popcorn, and regular size mugs. Although a taller overall microwave (due to controls running along the bottom rather than the side), it is limited in height space. So no extra tall mugs.

None of that is a big deal if you are just looking for basic reheating or popcorn popping.

Controls are easy enough, I won't describe them here. Default tapping is 30 second increments. Option to change that, change wattage, etc.

Given all that, I would give it a solid 4 stars.

Why the reduction to 1 star? Possible safety hazard and major inconvenience at times.

Occasionally while the microwave has been cooking something the cooking time on the microwave will suddenly change. I didn't ask ti to add time. It just decided to do so. I have had an item in there set for say 3 minutes (could be less, could be more), then hear it reset itself to 30 minutes. Certainly not anything that requires cooking for 30 minutes in a microwave. I am just reheating! Not always 30, sometimes a bit less, but the take away here is that it is doing something that wasn't asked of it. It just suddenly adds a bunch of time. I had always been in the room when this happens except this last time, which reminded me and prompted me to write a review. I decided to make a large portion of oatmeal in the microwave rather than stove top because I needed to make use of that time to take a quick shower rather than stand at a stove. I thought I could let the oats cook for 5 minutes with extra water; basically get them started and I would finish them off when I was done with showering. . I came back into the kitchen about 15 minutes later and the oats were still cooking. The microwave had an additional 28 minutes left according to read out (originally only set for 5). I immediately took the oats out and they were shriveled up to the point of being garbage. Had I not come back right away to check on it how long would this have cooked for? Would it just keep adding time? How much would it take to burn out the microwave or do house damage? This has happened the times that I have tried to make rice. Set for 15 minutes, and then it adds time. Or the readout starts flicking and flashing and beeping. I think the moisture affects the sensors. Have never experienced such odd behavior from a microwave until now. It needs to cook for what I set it at. No more, no less.

How about this? When you set the timer on the microwave, it successfully cooks what is in there, then turns off when timer runs out. Pretty basic expectation, right? If you leave food in there after the timer runs down it gives out a beep- like most microwaves- to let you know something is still in there. However, with this microwave, it doesn't always just stop there. This one has also on occasion just decided to turn itself back on, and setting the timer to some random number between 20-30 minutes. So the thing you only needed to cook for one minute is now being cooked for 20-30 minutes (and more?!?!) if you don't go grab it out from microwave immediately.

How about when it is not in use at all? Well, getting steam or other moisture (say from a cleaning product) on the control panel will make it beep and make the controls change (say from 5w to 75, etc).

I don't know.. it is just concerning. I'm trying to remember to unplug it now when not in use, and watch and listen very closely when it is in use. For these reasons, the potential safety hazard, and the decrease in convenience, I can't give it more than one star. Hope this helps.

EDIT: I added a picture. Note that the time remaining says 24+ minutes. I set it for ONLY five minutes! I was heating halved acorn squash. So what the...?

EDIT #2: I added a video- we were finally able to catch the concerning behavior on video. Once again, we do not leave food unattended in microwave, even if the timer has reached zero and turned off. The microwave will turn back on and set itself for maximum time (30 minutes!). Who knows how long it would continue to do that?! This was a food item put in for 3 minutes. The microwave cooked the food, then shut off at end of timer. My husband and I had been prepping other foods, so didn't take it out immediately, but within a minute, it turned back on and set itself for 30 minutes to cook. We stopped the microwave and decided to see if we could catch it doing it again, so we set it for a minute, and sure enough the microwave decided to turn back on shortly after and set itself for maximum cook time. Can you imagine if it did that and the food ws allowed to cook in a microwave for that long above and beyond what you intended? This was some cut up vegertables, but can you imagine popcorn? So yeh, we still use the microwave but we are aware of this bizarro behavior.
