Just so-so. Does this egg cooker cook? Yes it does. Does it do it well? No. The directions are really unclear, mostly because the measuring cup that measures the water, and the directions on how to use it are nonsensical. I read it several times when trying to make some hard boiled eggs. In the end, I had to just make my best guess. The same with the "poached" eggs.

I made two different kinds of eggs with this. I made 6 hard-boiled eggs and 2 "poached" eggs (cooked separately). First, the "poached" eggs. Why the quotation marks on "poached"? Because the directions tell you to smear the little poaching cups with butter. That is the way I cooked them, by following the directions. Most people poach eggs to avoid adding fat. I haven't tried to do it without butter. Don't know if it will stick to the cup or not. Either way, the eggs didn't cook evenly. There is a hot spot in the heating pan. One egg was cooked perfectly, and the other one was still had runny whites and was under done. I had to zap that one in the microwave for about 15 sec to finish the cooking. The unit DID shut off this time.

When I cooked the hard-boiled eggs, the water went completely dry, and it didn't shut off automatically like it is supposed to. It actually started to burn the bottom of the egg that sat over the hot spot. The shell turned brown from the heat. All the eggs were over-cooked, making the yolk chalky (instead of creamy) and gray all around the outside. Luckily, I had set a timer so I could check on it. The instructions said that it should take about 12 minutes. As I said, the unit didn't shut off when the water went dry and 12 minutes over-cooked the eggs. 10 minutes would have been better.

PROBLEMS:
1 - Unclear measurement markings.
2 - Hot spots on heating pan lead to uneven cooking.
3 - Automatic shut-off doesn't always shut off when the water goes dry.

Mounting bracket and hardware need fixing first. But the rack is great. The holes in the mounting bracket are placed in such a way that only one side attaches to a stud in the wall. The holes are wide enough apart that you would need a second stud in the wall next to it. So if you have the wall open or it is new construction, you are in luck. If you can remove a vertical strip of drywall/sheetrock and add in another 2x4 (even a shorter one) it would help a LOT.

I you can't, then figure out which direction side to side you will most often want to use the rack and mount the OTHER side into the stud. Do NOT use the provided anchors in the stud. (some are for masonry and some for drywall - either way, not for wood) Use heavy duty screws with wide heads (or washers so they don't slip through the holes)

For the other 2 holes, they will be in drywall. So use self-drilling plastic anchors (not molly bolts)
https://www.amazon.com/Drilling-Drywall-Plastic-Anchors-Screws/dp/B09P4JPFB8/ref=sr_1_4?crid=HBH14L538CFS&keywords=heavy%2Bduty%2BSelf%2BDrilling%2BDrywall%2BPlastic%2BAnchors&qid=1659391929&s=hi&sprefix=heavy%2Bdutyself%2Bdrilling%2Bdrywall%2Bplastic%2Banchors%2Ctools%2C160&sr=1-4&th=1

Works Well But Surface Gets a Little Too Hot. This is my first exposure to electric kettles, having used a whistling tea kettle for many years. While it seems to work very well and it does what it is supposed to do I found that some caution is required when using it due to surface and steam heat.

The idea of this type of kettle is very straightforward - it contains an integrated hot plate in the bottom of the kettle that heats up quickly and is used specifically for boiling water. Because of the low wattage it draws less electricity than using a stove top kettle or the microwave and because of the rapid heating it boils water very quickly which saves time.

I have used the kettle to heat a small amount of water and to heat the full kettle's worth and understandably it takes longer to heat more. This should not be a huge surprise. That said, it still works quickly and the water boils in a lot less time than when heated up in a microwave (which I find to be faster than the stove top). It does a great job of getting the water boiling quickly and without risking a spill.

In spite of its usefulness in saving time and energy, I have two reservations when it comes to using this kettle. My first observation is that the surface of the kettle's pitcher gets very hot, to the point of discomfort when you touch it. Well, of course it's going to get warm but the fact that it gets as warm as it does concerns me. It would have been nice if the pitcher was better insulated (or, rather, insulated at all). More unpleasant, though, is that after the water is hot if you open the top for pouring a cloud of steam tends to billow out and it's a little too easy to get a steam burn if caution is not used. Sure, you should not stick your hand in there and it should be obvious that there will be steam but the fact that it comes straight up and out is concerning.

This is not a bad kettle. It's actually a nice product and it works as advertised. Unfortunately, it needs a design revisit.

Very Nice Crockpot, But Not Really Programmable. We use crock pots in our house almost weekly for the convenience and for their ability to tenderize meats. I have used mostly Rival and Hamilton Beach crock pots but I am familiar with several other brands, but Bella is a brand which which I was previously unfamiliar. My impression of this crock pot is positive, but it is not programmable as it has been advertised.

Most crockpots have either two or three temperature settings - warm, low and high. The Bella crockpot has three, and all of these work as one would expect. There's no rocket science here - the element heats the ceramic liner to a specific temperature and maintains that temperature through cooking.

This is an easy to use crockpot that heats nicely and does a good job. It seems to cook at proper temperatures and it does not get too hot to touch on the surface. The lid fits nicely too, which is a plus. Things we have made with this crock pot have turned out right so far.

This particular is touted as being programmable, but it isn't. Instead, it has digital settings control with a built in countdown timer. So, for example you can set it to cook on low for 8 hours through the use of some button settings. When the time is up, the crock put turns off completely. The programmable crock pots I have seen switch to the warm setting after the time is up, which makes better sense. Any advantage to having a digital control is lost if it is unable to change modes automatically.

Another oversight in the controls is that there is no notification that the time is up. A sound alerting the user that it has completed the cycle would be a nice thing if it's not going to change modes, but this is not there either. So, a user must be conscious of when the crock pot is actually going to finish. This really defeats the whole purpose of having a timer on it, and it actually is a negative. If the user isn't aware of when it cuts off, there may be cold food waiting for dinner.

This is a decent crock pot and it looks nice. Some real thought went into the design of the appliance and the digital controls are easy to use. It is unfortunate that the timer and programmability aspects just aren't there for the user. If you want a programmable crock pot, look for other options. If you don't mind keeping track of cooking times and paying attention to how much time is left on the timer, this is not a bad device.

Decent Set but Lacks Fit and Finish. Westinghouse is not a name I would have ever associated with cookware. Until now, in my mind the Westinghouse brand meant electronics and in particular light bulbs. I was curious to see how well this cast iron cookware would compare to Lodge and Griswold/Wagner, and so far I have found it to be less than great. It is a good dutch oven/skillet set, but it lacks in the fit-and-finish.

This is a 3-quart dutch oven with a 10” skillet for the lid. This is a great combination and makes fine use of an otherwise wasted lid. I have used cast iron skillets and dutch ovens for years, and I especially like the way cast iron retains heat and also how it heats evenly. It is more consistent than aluminum, and it does not leech aluminum into the things you cook (it leeches iron, which is better for you). The trade-off is a lot heavier than most other cookware.

These are marketed as pre-seasoned, and that is not entirely accurate though it is consistent with other manufacturers’ labeling. This set does have an initial coating toward pre-seasoning but this is not sufficient to prevent things from sticking. Plan to season this set again after washing it. This is not unique to this set; I would give the same advice for Lodge pans that have been pre-seasoned.

My main issue with this set is the fact that it is very rough surfaced and feels like sandpaper. If you plan to cook something like eggs in the skillet, plan to spend a good bit of time cleaning it with a stiff brush over and over until there is a very thick layer of seasoning. For vegetables, oily fools like sausage, spaghetti sauces and other things, it’s fine. This is not an excuse though - it should have been sanded and made more smooth (and thus more suitable for frying) prior to leaving the factory. This is fixable if you have the tools to sand down the rough surface and then season it properly, but it should not have to be this way.

This is not a bad set and it definitely has its uses. However, there are better choices available.

Entry Level Gaming Chair. I selected this item for my son who is a gamer and spends a good bit of time in front of the computer. It’s a rocker style gaming chair, a style of chair with which I was previously unfamiliar, and I was hopeful that it would be an enjoyable accessory for him. A lot of other gaming chairs have this kind of configuration. I’ll confess to being skeptical of the vibration feedback in particular but I did not have high expectations for the speakers either (based on having worked with dozens of Bluetooth speakers over time). Instead of being a typical stand chair, this is a rocker which sits on the floor - not suitable at all for sitting at a desk. It’s reasonably lightweight and easy to move so taking it to another room is easy enough. It is bulky, though, so this is not the kind of accessory that you’d pack up and carry to a friend’s house.

Bluetooth connection is straightforward and easy and we had no issues connecting to phones, tablets or even the PC. It uses an older Bluetooth standard so there should be little issue with support. Once connected, the speakers kick in like you’d expect.

We discovered a couple of issues that make this less than ideal. First, the chair itself comes in the box and folded in half, and Velcro is used to fix the chair into a fully upright position. That’s ok, except that the Velcro is a weak point and it’s a matter of time before it weakens. The chair isn’t all that expensive so it isn’t a huge loss if the stitching around the Velcro fatigues, but be aware. Second, the speaker quality met expectations and is relatively mediocre. Finally, the vibration feedback isn’t all that effective and seems more of an afterthought.

This is not a terrible chair, but I hesitate to call it particularly good. I would call it a reasonable entry-level chair at an entry-level price.

Assembly Issues and Won't Stay Mounted. My wife has been after me to hang up a paper power holder for a while and this looked like a good one that would fill the need we have. Unfortunately we have encountered a couple of issues with it. In a nutshell, we’ve have an assembly issue and the thing just will not stay mounted.

Right out of the box, the bar where the paper towel roll goes was loose – very loose. There are two screws that attach this bar to the rest of the assembly, and one of them had worked loose. Not a big deal, it’s easy enough to tighten. However, it loosened up again and I had to tighten it a second time. This is no good.

Mounting this holder involves using the sticky pads and either glue or double sided tape to attach it to the surface where it is to be mounted. In theory this is a good approach, but in practice there are some issues. I have been trying for several days to mount it on a glossy tile surface in my kitchen, and it just will not stay attached. I have tried multiple types of double-sided tape, including one brand that is rated to handle up to 30 pounds, and it still pulls away from the holder (it sticks to the tile just fine).

For the moment, it sits on its end on the counter. That’s not a particularly useful way to get the paper towel roll off the counter and out of the way.

Room for Improvement: Needs a Better Lid. I selected this coffee tumbler because we do go through coffee in the house and a tumbler this size is good for making iced coffee drinks (for those that like that kind of stuff) and for those that like a big cup of coffee (that would be me). This cup is not ideal; the main issue I have with it is the lid.

First off, this is a very large tumbler. The average I have seen in tumbler size is 20-24oz. This one is a full 30 ounces and that’s a lot of coffee if you fill it up. That’s not a problem at all, but be aware of this before you purchase. I like this size because it allows me to put the amount of coffee in that I want and leave some room at the top to add creamer if I want it and to put the lid on without spilling.

Ah, the lid… This is the weak spot in this tumbler. The lid has a slider that opens up the lid to reveal an inadequately small hole through which the coffee flows. I found myself frustrated quickly with this and I replaced the lid with one from another tumbler, after which all was right in the world. This is unfortunate; almost every lid I have gotten with other tumblers – including smaller ones – has a larger drinking hole in the top.

Another issue which does not affect me much but will definitely be a problem for others is the shape of the tumbler itself. Most I have seen have been shaped such that a third-party handle can be attached and the tumbler then can be carried around like a regular coffee mug. The smooth sides don’t permit that. If you have to have a handle for your coffee cup, this one will not do. This is a personal preference, and probably impacts those who drink coffee in the car more than anyone else.

Finally – mine came with a nice dent in it. Doesn’t affect usability, but it’s still very unfortunate and I'm not happy.

There is room for improvement with this tumbler. The size is great for me, though some might not want one this big. The lid needs to be rethought, though, which is the biggest problem with it.

Trades Power for Convenience. My wife has been after me for a vacuum cleaner like this that is small, lightweight and is easy to handle. I selected this one for her and we spent an evening testing it out and putting it through its paces. It has some excellent qualities but we were both disappointed with it in several areas.

Taking this fellow out of the box, it comes disassembled to save space in shipping. Assembly took less than 5 minutes, and most of the time spent was taking the parts out of the box and getting them out of the protective plastic. That was a good sign right off the bat.

This is an extremely lightweight unit, even with the battery installed. It is definitely easy to handle and that’s excellent for her, as she doesn’t like pushing around our heavy Dyson. When it’s broken down and being used as a small convenience vacuum, such as for doing the stairs or working in the car it is even more lightweight. This one gets high marks for the size and weight.

Our first task for this vacuum was the linoleum kitchen floor, and it did a fantastic job with it. We ran it on low power, and it managed to pick up almost everything, the exceptions being things that were stuck down and had to be scraped from the floor. Because of the size and the swivel action of the head, it is super easy to maneuver around corners, along the cabinetry and under chairs and tables. We kicked on the “turbo” mode and it didn’t seem to make any difference in this scenario – not a big deal, just a data point. Even when on full power, we were pleased with how quiet this vacuum cleaner is compared to our corded upright.

We moved over to the carpet and hit a high-traffic area, and as we predicted it did a fair job but not as good a job as our Dyson. I expected that a battery-powered vacuum would trade the convenience for power, and I was right, though it did well enough to pick up most visible debris from the carpet.

Where this vacuum really showed its compromise in power, though, was when we decided to clean cat hair from the couch. We have two cats, and they love our cloth-covered couch, so there’s plenty of hair to vacuum away on any given day. We converted the vacuum to a handheld, attached the upholstery head, put it on high power and proceeded to vacuum the couch cushions. It did a fair job, but it left as much as it collected and we reverted to a different vacuum to finish the job.

When finished, we emptied the collection bin, and this proved to be the easiest vacuum to empty of any we have used. Press a button on the side to pop open the canister door, and simply dump out the contents into a plastic bag. It doesn’t require partial disassembly or anything. It is smaller than most, of course, so it will not collect as much.

We ran the battery completely out of power and plugged it in to charge. It literally took 5 hours to go from completely empty to fully-charged. That’s a lot of time to charge the battery, to get 30-45 minutes of run time! That requires some planning ahead when using this unit. In light of this, I looked into getting a second battery, and was startled to find that batteries are presently selling for $100. That’s 1/3 the cost of the vacuum itself. I was hoping the battery would instead cost $50-$60, which to me is a reasonable cost. On the plus side, the battery does not need to be in the vacuum cleaner itself to be charged.

This vacuum cleaner is an interesting unit. It has some excellent qualities, among them being size and weight and the ability to convert to a hand-held with no cord, but it has some downsides too, such as the battery cost and the lack of power in certain circumstances. I can’t say this is a bad unit, but consider how you’d use it: if you’ll be using it on hardwood or linoleum, it’s really great, but if you want to use it on carpet of furniture it struggles to perform. Also weigh the cost/convenience of buying a second battery – it’s an appreciable chunk of money for a fairly short runtime.

Limited Usefulness, Depending on Size/Shape of the Bread. I have been making artisan loaves of bread for over 20 years to feed my family and to share with friends and coworkers. Sandwich loaves are easy to store – put them in a plastic bag and they’ll stay soft. Baguettes and peasant loaves are another issue: those should stay crusty on the outside and when stored in plastic they soften quickly. Their odd shape also makes is awkward to store them as well. These bread savers are a solution to that. They’re not ideal but they work well enough and they seem to be made well.

The idea is simple. Instead of wrapping the loaves in plastic wrap, these rubber caps go over the end of the loaves to keep the sliced ends from getting stale while leaving the uncut end exposed to air, allowing it to remain crisp. In theory this is ideal. However, there are a couple of issues, neither are deal breakers but should be kept in mind. First, these are basically sleeves and the portion of the crust that is covered will soften. This is unavoidable but is better than having a squishy loaf. Second, these are not one-size-fits all. They are stretchy and will fit over the ends of most peasant loaves, but they will not fit over a traditional baguette (they’re too large to stay on) and they will not work for large boules (wrong shape and often too small). For the average peasant loaf or Italian loaf, though, these work well enough.

I’m on the fence with these. They answer a need for keeping bread from staling on the ends, but the size and shape limits their use.

Budget Quality Cutlery. Farberware is not a name I associate with high-end cookware and utensils. That said, I have had good fortune with most of their cookware and I looked to this set as a decent budget set for general cooking. For the price it’s an acceptable set but I would not look to it to last for a long time.

There are three tools in this set – a chef’s knife, a paring knife and a pair of kitchen shears. Right out of the package they’re sharp and ready to go (I’d suggest washing them first, of course). I do not know yet how quickly they’ll dull.

The handles are molded plastic and there is a visible seam on each. That in itself does not concern me but is a clear indicator that these are budget-line utensils. The blades, though, are not full tang and without a little care this can fatigue the handle when each is used. I have visions of the chef’s knife in particular breaking in mid-use when chopping.

I can recommend this set with some reservations. It’s a budget-friendly set of tools for the kitchen that makes a decent starter set, but I question its durability.

Expensive. This is a nice matching towel set, containing two bath towels, two hand towels, and four wash cloths. While I like this set and they’re good towels, I have a couple of concerns about them.

Overall this is a decent set. The color is uniform and I have found no faded spots or miscolorations. The stitching is straight and I have not seen any issues with pilling, loose loops or uneven materials. I haven’t found any real issues with the workmanship.

That said, these do shed lint in the dryer, to a point that I’d recommend some caution when throwing them in with items of dissimilar colors. The lint screen in the dryer catches a lot of lint from these towels, at least in the initial washings, and what it doesn’t catch ends up on other articles.

The second concern I have is the cost of this set. It’s not inexpensive and I am not sure the cost is justified when compared to similar sets available. Don’t get me wrong, these are very definitely better than the cheap sets you can find at national budget department stores, but I’d hesitate to say they are better enough to justify the price differential.

This is a good set of towels. They match nicely and they are well made. I question if the asking price is justified though, and I would recommend caution when tossing them in the dryer with other items.

Not Airtight. Note: There are several products attached to this listing. I am specifically writing this review for the 10-lb./5 L. container.

I selected this container initially with the idea of keeping my wife’s popcorn in it. She loves her popcorn and so far we have not had a good way to store it. Because she likes pre-popped popcorn for the convenience, this container seemed like a good solution for her, allowing her better access than bags and should seal better. I found this not to be the case – this container is not air-tight and does not seal as well as I’d hoped.

I will start with one thing about this container that seems a little counter-intuitive at first. The lid has a handle and the lid seals when the handle is down. This seems a bit backward at first – I expected the lid to seal with the handle up for carrying. However, this is a good arrangement because the container is designed for stacking, and when I considered that it made more sense. It’s not a design problem at all when considered in that way. With 10 pounds of rice in the container, the handle likely would strain under the weight anyway.

This is a generous sized container and it can hold quite a bit. It’s sufficient for storing most dry goods, like rice, popcorn, flour, sugar, and coffee beans.

My issue with this container isn’t the design but the implementation. To be blunt, the lid does not seal tightly. Even when “locked” with the handle down, and after watching the locking mechanism move the gasket, it is very easy to simply pop the top off, with very little resistance. Depending on what you’re sealing in and why will determine if this is good or bad. On one hand the seal is sufficient to keep out insects and other contaminants, but it is not enough to keep the contents free of humidity and certainly not sufficient to keep the lid secure if the container is dropped. So, if what you’re putting in has a tendency to get stale when exposed to moisture, this might not be the best solution.

This is a nice container that holds a lot, but it doesn’t seal as nicely as it should and that can be a real issue depending on what’s inside. For rice, it’s probably just fine when in a dry area, but for things like flour and sugar it’s probably going to disappoint.

Inconsistent Results. I have had trouble with sleep for years and I have tried numerous things to get better sleep, with limited success. Though this device isn’t a sleep aid, it is a sleep monitor (of sorts) and I looked to it in the hopes of finding some clues about my rest patterns at night. I came away disappointed, though it does have some useful/interesting features.

This seems like a very unconventional device for a sleep study. It’s basically a pad with sensors talking to software on a portable device, via Bluetooth. I am not thrilled with the idea of using my phone to monitor me all night long, though I am less concerned about using this with a tablet.

Like others, I had some real trouble getting this thing to read correctly and it gave me very inconsistent results. Following the advice given by other reviewers, I was not able to get it to read completely reliably, though positioning farther towards the center of the bed made it read a little more consistently. It was worth trying. I’m still trying to get it to play ball a little more reliably.

The software seems to be well thought out and is fairly intuitive.

As it stands, this device seems to be a good idea with some room for improvement. Based on my experiences I am having a difficult time recommending it because I cannot get it to work as it should. If I am successful in getting it to read and report properly, I will revisit.

Nice Glassware for the Toaster Oven, but of Limited Use. Note: There is more than one product attached to this listing. I am specifically writing this review for the 6-piece set.

I have a nice toaster oven and I have on occasion wished I could use it more efficiently as an oven instead of just a toaster and broiler. These actually fit my toaster oven nicely and will see more use. That said, there are some limitations.

As another reviewer stated, these are not borosilicate glass, but rather are coke lime glass. That's usually not a problem, but it does mean the heat tolerances are lower than older Pyrex glassware. Most significantly it means these are not safe to go directly from the freezer to the oven. Using them that way can result in shatterrd glass and a big mess to clean up.

These are smaller, low-profile glass dishes that fit nicely in a toaster oven. They're unusual sizes though, and I have found very few recipes that call for these smaller sizes of dishes. They're perhaps useful for breaking recipes into two dishes but then you'll have to play with the bake times. Keep this in mind. On the other hand, these are useful when making smaller batches of roasted vegetables and similar things, where a recipe isn't followed and the quantity is kept small.

Being glass, these are not hard to clean when you have finished with them. They are dishwasher safe, and it is safe to put some muscle behind them when scrubbing when there's something stubborn stuck on them. They do not stack particularly well, but even so they're small enough to tuck away in less convenient places on shelves and cabinets that are too small for bigger dishes.

I do like these, and I do make use of them, but I can see limited usefulness because of the small and unusual sizes. Typical recipes need to be scaled and cook times adjusted to make these work.

Attractive but Flawed Pan. I love cooking with cast-iron cookware and I have a modest collection of pots and pans. This is my first enameled frying pan, and I will be honest, it is disappointing. It works well enough but the fit and finish is lacking.

This pan is actually quite attractive. It is glazed red on the outside such that it looks like it is weathered and heavily used even though it's brand new. The inside is black; I have seen some enameled pans that are white, and I mention the color more as a data point than anything else.

It has a good weight to it - less weighty than my standard 10.5" cast iron skillet, though it outweighs my carbon steel pan. The handle is a good length and the helper handle makes transport easy.

Where I have difficulty with this pan is in the finish. The lip around the edge of the pan is actually not glazed and is exposed cast iron. This is easy enough to season, though doesn't seem like much thought went into it. My particular pan itself has a defect that can be seen on the top and bottom, though, almost like something flat and mostly round was used to pick up the pan while it was still hot. It does not affect usability but it is visibly obvious. The glaze on the cooking surface, though, is the biggest disappointment. It feels gritty like unseasoned cast iron and it is not as non-stick (even with butter or oil) as it should be as a result.

This pan is useful for cooking when the benefit of using glazed cast iron isn't really needed. An example is in making English muffins or similar goods that do not require oil.

This is an attractive pan and I will get some use out of it, but the fit and finish are lacking. The cost is low, and the quality is on par with the cost.

Read the Documentation. I selected this roasting pan with Thanksgiving turkey in mind. I have a shallow roasting pan that I have used and it does work but it is a nightmare to clean and is so low-profile that I worry about losing what I'm cooking when I am moving it. While I like this pan, the warnings that come with give me pause.

First off, it is very clearly marketed as a steel pan. This is one of the reasons I selected it as I am not too excited about using aluminum (and given the choice, I would use cast iron exclusively). For a steel pan, this one is very lightweight, more so than I could reasonably expect.

One of the big factors for me when when selecting cookware is whether or not it is coated in Teflon. This doesn't look like a Teflon-coated pan, but the warning label hits all the check boxes - keep away from pets and small children while not in use, and it doesn't mean that the pan gets hot and can cause burns. In fact, it spells out the potential for respiratory issues when this pan is being used - a problem with Teflon when it is heated to a certain threshold and beyond. With two cats in the house, there is cause for concern in light of the warnings.

As a large serving pan, though, I have found it to be more than sufficient. The handles make it easy to control and carry, and it's spacious enough to hold a lot.

So, this is not the roasting pan I will be using for Thanksgiving. It seems to be made well enough (though I question the material claims), it is easy to clean and it looks nice. However, the warnings that come with it are enough to make me wary. My search for a better roasting pan continues.

Not Great on Carpet; Lightweight. I selected this vacuum cleaner with the hopes that it would be a suitable replacement for a very cheap and inexpensive upright vacuum cleaner. I’ve had good experiences with Black+Decker tools as well as kitchen appliances, so part of my reason for selecting it was based on brand recognition. It has been a big let-down and I can’t recommend this vacuum cleaner without reservation except in specific cases and for specific uses.

Almost everything about this vacuum feels like it was made with lower-quality materials, the exception being the metal extending tube which is actually solid and well-made. The plastic tubing to which it attaches is cheap and is held to the metal tube only by friction, not unlike pipe fitting without adhesives. The attachments also feel substandard, and the housing feels lightweight.

The main attachment which is used for carpet and hardwood is probably the biggest issue with this whole system. It does not work smoothly on carpet and it takes real effort to get it to roll. I thought perhaps I had the lever on it set wrong (the lever moves the leading brush which is useful for pet hair), and that wasn’t it – moving the lever so it protruded the brush made it appreciably worse. I did figure out that on carpet, turning down the power does make it roll better, but then the suction is reduced and it doesn’t pick up as well anyway. Slightly larger wheels would solve this issue, I think.

When using with the edge attachment or small brush, this vacuum becomes a serious contender. This has a lot of power and it can definitely suck up dirt and debris from small spaces. I did not understand the reasoning behind the variable speeds – at first. Once I realized that full power is not always ideal, I got better results and found the unit easier to maneuver. The power level also affects loudness too so it can be operated at slower speeds when quieter operation is desired.

When the metal extension is removed from the mix, this vacuum works quite well as a car vacuum. It is powerful enough to get most things out of the flooring and from between the seat and base. The brush works well for dusting the dash as well. It’s also excellent on hardwood floors and linoleum where there is no carpet with which to contend.

The unit is lightweight and relatively easy to carry. It is not as easy to carry as a cordless upright, but it is not a tank either.

I have mixed feelings about this vacuum cleaner. On one hand, it does a sub-optimal job on carpet due to the design of the floor attachment and the overall unit feels of substandard quality. On the other hand, it is good on non-carpet floors and it has plenty of power. Your mileage may vary. For me, this isn’t my first choice when I need to vacuum my living room but is my go to when I want to clean my car.

Falls Short. I selected this blanket as a solution to an issue we have had regarding "differences of opinion" regarding the proper temperature setting on the thermostat. I selected it with the hope that it would be lightweight and still warm enough to take off the chill when the temperature is low at night. It does help but it is not the full solution to the issue at hand.

First off, this looks like a thermal blanket but it does not work as well as a true thermal blanket. The weave is nice and it has a nice waffle pattern in the fabric, but it does not retain the heat as we hoped. A fleece throw (even a fake one made of synthetic material) works better at retaining heat.

To be fair, this is a decent blanket and it does work as an added layer when trying to get warm at night. As a single layer thought it leaves much to be desired.

There has been some discussion about if it shrinks when it is washed and dried. So far we have not laundered this blanket so I do not know yet if it will shrink. I received the king size for use on a queen or twin bed so shrinkage will not be an issue in my case, but that is only because I am using it on a smaller bed.

This is a decent blanket in it's own right, but it is mis-marketed as a thermal blanket when it doesn't retain heat like a thermal blanket should. It's a good solution if adding layers, but as a stand-alone blanket it falls short.

Grinds Too Fine. I selected this coffee grinder to speed the process of grinding coffee in the house. I have another grinder that I use but it is smaller capacity and is quite noisy. I was hopeful this one would prove to be better and would work faster. It’s a mixed bag for me.

This is a burr grinder as opposed to a blade grinder so the coffee does come out more uniform than if using a blade-based solution, since the beans have to pass through the burr to get to the storage reservoir after processing. The grinding process also is significantly quieter than when using my blade grinder which is a big plus and one of the reasons I selected it. The capacity can be varied so you can grind enough beans for 2 cups, 18 cups, or anywhere in between.

The unit disassembles easily enough for cleaning which is good. It even comes with a small brush for getting into the reservoir where the beans are ground (not where the grounds are deposited, though it will help a little there too).

The main issue I have with this grinder is the coarseness setting. It is supposed to allow for grinding beans coarsely for a French press or very fine for espresso, with varying degrees of grit in between. On the most coarse setting it still grinds the beans quite finely, almost to a soft powder and totally unusable for my French press and nearly borderline for my drip coffee maker. I haven’t found a way to adjust this any more than just using the coarseness knob.

I like this grinder but I have reservations about recommending it. It would be so much more useful and effective if the coarseness setting was more accurate and was more in line with where it should be. It’ll work great if you want espresso or cappuccino, and it works acceptably for drip makers, but it’s a non-starter if you use a French press.

A Little Too Small. I selected this little support pillow with the thought that my wife would appreciate it on a trip we were taking across the country. It’s billed as a lumbar support pillow but it is suitable for neck support as well. After working with it for a few weeks, we both have come to the conclusion that it’s not quite right for us, though it likely will work fine for others.

This is a duffel-shaped pillow, filled with buckwheat hulls. It’s approximately a foot long and about as big around as a 2-liter soda bottle. Unlike memory foam, this pillow holds its volume a bit and as such it provides decent support for the lumbar portion of your back or for your neck.

The problem we found with it is the very thing that others will appreciate – the size. The volume is good, but the length is a touch short and we’ve both found ourselves having to adjust it when we move in the chair or car seat. The straps do allow for securing the pillow so it doesn’t shift, but there are no buckles, so it requires additional planning.

This isn’t a bad pillow, but for us it is not ideal.

Expensive and Difficult to Access the Filter. I drink a lot of coffee and I have noticed the differences when coffee beans are fresh and when they go rancid. It's unpleasant, to say the least. I selected this container with the idea of keeping the coffee fresher longer. I have not had it long enough to know how effective it will be in the long run, but I do have some observations to share about it.

This is a stainless steel sealing jar with a latch lid and a silicone gasket to keep air out. I like the overall appearance and the feel of it. It comes with a little scoop too which is nice when you are using this jar to store grounds (not so much for whole beans). It has a nifty dial on the top that you can use to mark when you last filled the jar or when you need to empty it, as appropriate.

When I selected this jar I thought it would have a pump of some kind to extract air. That was my mistake. What this jar does is allow air out via a filter valve in the lid. That's fine and it is clear in the product description; it was my misunderstanding the design. Included are two extra filters.

I have two problems with this jar. First, it is expensive for what it is. Other similar steel jars are less expensive, which puts this one at a disadvantage. More importantly, though, it is unclear how to access the filter in the lid and as such there's no easy path for changing it. With no instructions in the box, I have not been able to figure out how to replace the filter that's installed prior to shipment. It looks like the cover holding it in place is supposed to twist to unlock, but it is so tight that I cannot get it to budge and I am unwilling to use tools for concern of damaging it.

I think this jar is a workable solution but there are a couple of things about it that give me some pause. The price is one, and the difficulty (?) of replacing the filter is another. If I figure out how to access the filter so it can be changed, I will will return here and update.

Odd Shapes; How are they Measured?. Note: There are several products attached to this listing. I am specifically reviewing the 3-pack of bakeware.

My experience with Rubbermaid has been with trash cans and storage containers. This is my first experience with their bakeware and to be honest I am underwhelmed. These have a strange shape to them and may be off a bit on the sizes.

The listing says these are 13"x9", 12"x8", and 8"x8". The issue is that these are not exactly squared off and have odd shapes with curved sides. It is unclear how these are then measured, but even so it become even less clear if these are actually the stated sizes. Are they measured from the corners where the dishes are narrower than the sides, or from the center of each edge where they're widest? Either way, it would skew the size. Maybe there's some weird average taken for each side measurement?

These are definitely lightweight and are easy to clean, though. Compared to a glass 13"x9" dish these are definitely quite a bit lighter and easier to handle. They're a lot easier to wash too which is a nice plus. And, they're dishwasher safe.

I have mixed feelings about these baking dishes. They're made to be lightweight and easy to clean, and in that regard they succeed wonderfully. However, they are shaped a little differently and there's some question regarding their stated sizes.

Light Duty. Years ago we were gifted a breakfast tray similar to this one. We still use it frequently and we have needed another one. I was excited to try this one out. Unfortunately, it isn't quite as nice as I'd hoped.

I'll get right to the point - this is not as sturdy a tray as it should be. The legs are thin and are susceptible to breaking if the tray is dropped or mishandled. It is not going to simply collapse under its own weight, and it is made well enough for light duty, but it is not something on which I would rely.

Otherwise, this is an attractive tray. It is large enough to handle a dinner plate with some room to spare and it is natural colored so it looks nice. The legs are attached well and they to not swing loosely.

This is an attractive and functional tray, but I have some reservations. Time will tell it if is sturdier than it seems.

Great Bottle But Very Overpriced. I prefer glass bottles to plastic and metal, so the Soma water bottle is a good choice for me. It’s made well and it looks great. The only reservation I have about it – the price.

The bottle is heavy glass borosilicate. This particular type of glass is somewhat more resistant to shattering, though its strength is in being fairly impervious to rapid temperature changes. This bottle is not designed to be used for hot beverages so I suspect it could have been made with a lower grade of glass and still be shatter-resistant. It’s not unwelcome, either way. Because it is glass and not plastic, it doesn’t stain which is great when you fill it with something colorful and fair to wash it afterward – it still comes clean.

The bottle has a rubbery sleeve that serves two purposes. First, it is an insulator and it will keep you from freezing your hands when drinking something very cold. Second, if your hands are wet it is still sufficient to help you maintain a good, solid grip on the bottle.

The cap is the weak point though it is relative. It is plastic on the inside, with a heavy bamboo outer shell to protect it. It will likely survive it you drop it, though it seems like this is the one part that is most likely to fail. So far, I have used the bottle and kept the cap on a nearby shelf, so I don’t have an opportunity to drop it but this is more so I won’t actually misplace it.

Decent Cutting Surface and Interesting Design, but Room for Improvement. I selected this cutting board set with the thought of using with with less countertop mess. It has not worked out quite like I envisioned. There are some design decisions that went into this product that merit a revisit.

This is a bamboo-surface cutting board with enough room to handle some of the larger jobs you might have in the kitchen - trimming a steak, cutting up butternut squash, breaking down a pineapple, and so on. I have no complaints with the size or the cutting surface which is smooth and not easily gashed without a serrated knife. Under the cutting surface are two steel catch bins with is great for prep work.

Where this product falls short is in two areas. First, it would have been useful to have a canal for draining off the juice trap. As received, the juice trap canal has no channel for drainage, so when it's full it just overflows. To drain it, it either needs to be inverted or the liquid needs to be mopped out. Second, this unit will not store compactly with the bamboo lids on the catch trays. Either the trays have to be removed for separate storage, or the tray lids stored upside down on top of the cutting board. Neither is ideal.

This is not a bad cutting board system, but there is room for improvement. The design is interesting and the craftmanship is fine, but minor oversights tarnish this enough from being a great product.

Just Too Small. Note: There are multiple products attached to this listing. I am specifically reviewing the 0.55lb. pan with striped lid.

I have been baking breads from scratch for many years and I was very interested in trying this pan, especially after recently breaking one of my glass loaf pans. I have worked with other Chefmade pans and each I have used has been of good quality and worked well, so I had elevated expectations. I was surprised when this loaf pan arrived – it’s much smaller than I expected.

First, the positives. This is a nice little pan that seems to be very well-made. It feels solid, and the non-stick surface (not Teflon) feels almost slippery. Nothing is going to stick to this pan. I have not tried this, but I believe I could make hard candy in this little pan and it would not stick. Breads baked in this pan slip right out and are properly browned on all sides. It’s easy to clean.

However… This loaf pan is about 4.5” square which makes a very, very small loaf, too small for much more than novelty presentation or making in large quantities for gifting (and then you need multiple pans anyway). I did not realize it would be as small at it is before it arrived.

For me, this pan is just too small to be useful. The larger size might be more in line with what I would use. If you like small, gifting-sized loaves that look really nice and you like non-stick bakeware, this is a decent option. If you’re making bread to make a week’s worth of sandwiches, this isn’t the best choice.

Works Well but Needs a Design Revisit. The best slow cooker I have used has been a Hamilton Beach Stay or Go, so I was excited to try this new one by Hamilton Beach. It has an interesting feature set and it works well, but I dislike some of the design decisions.

The listing states that this is a stainless steel crock pot, and that’s true when referring to the outer body of the cooker. The liner itself is aluminum (a detail that is not highlighted but is mentioned in the listing) and is coated in some kind of non-stick material (not sure if it’s Teflon). That’s ok, but that needs to be more clearly described. The liner is very lightweight and is easy to handle and easy to clean. Being the clumsy person that I am, it means I can’t drop it and break it like I can with a stoneware crock.

This is a 6-quart cooker, so it can handle a full pot roast or roasting bird. Unlike the Stay or Go line, the lid does not lock in place – that’s ok, if you do not need to transport the cooker anywhere. Because the lid does not lock in place for transport, it’s a simpler design and easier to clean.

It happened to arrive on a day when I needed to use the slow cooker for dinner. Instead of using my Stay or Go, I used this one instead. Dinner turned out exactly as expected and this cooker did a good job.

However, there are a couple of things about this cooker that turn me off. First, the controls are not granular enough. You can set the temperature to Low, High and Warm at the press of a button which is great, but you cannot set the time in any less than 2-hour increments, up to 10 hours. If you need to put something in for any other interval, there isn’t any way to do it. Second, the cooker has absolutely no time display so you have no indicator of how much time remains. It does change the time setting as the time counts down, so it shows what two-hour block it’s in during the cook cycle. Whether there are 2 hours or 5 minutes left, it says “2 hours”. Finally, the outer surface is definitely less insulated that any other slow cooker I have used and with no effort at all I got a first-degree burn on my hand. The liner gets hotter than a stoneware crock too and it’s easy to get a wicked burn in no time.

This isn’t a bad cooker, but there are some design decisions with which I disagree than make it a less-than-ideal choice. The controls and display need a revisit. A little better unsulation on the outer part of the cooker would be greatly appreciated. And to be honest, I would rather have seen the liner be made of uncoated stainless steel instead of coated aluminum. It does work well and it’s easy to clean which are pluses, but to me these are not enough to counter the negatives. This is a cooker I will use when I need a backup or more than one at a time – I’ll stick with the Stay or Go as my go-to slow cooker.

Room for Improvement. I have wanted a fat fryer for a while and I was pleased to have the opportunity to try this one. For the most part I am pleased with it but I do see a couple of areas for improvement.

This is a generous-sized fryer, holding about 1 gallon of oil. That’s a generous size for making all kinds of good things like onion rings, fries, or my favorite, oysters. It has dual controls for time and temperature that are very easy to understand and very easy to operate. It has a lid that closes over the baskets so splatter is minimized during the cooking process and there are ridges on the baskets so they can be clamped above the hot oil to drip off excess fat before serving. Overall, the design is nice.

I have made three observations that leave room for improvement, though none of these are deal breakers:

1. This unit takes quite a while to heat up. Do not expect to turn it on and have hot oil 5 minutes later.

2. There are two baskets, but one large oil chamber. So, you can cook two things at once, but if they’re not the same thing you can get mixed flavors. A good case in point is shrimp and fried potatoes. The potatoes will come out tasting like shrimp. It would have been nice to have either a permanent division between them or a removable partition so that you can cook things together if you want or separately.

3. The baskets are very, very cheap. When I took the fryer out of the box I could not use the baskets until I bent them back into shape so they’d fit. I understand that they do not need to be solid, heavy wire frame baskets, but they should not be so flexible that they get misshapen in shipping. This is my biggest disappointment with this fryer so far.

Overall, I am happy with this fryer but there is very definitely room for improvement. It works well, it is easy to understand and use and it produces good results. But, there’s enough improvement that can be made to give me pause.

Not High Quality; Suitable as a Starter Set. Normally when I think of Cuisinart I think of a better-than-average brand in cookware and appliances, and I have had some good experiences with their products over the years. Of late, though, I have seen a decline in the quality of their offerings, in particular their utensils (their frying pans are still better than average). Unfortunately, this set has some of the same shortcomings I have seen from other Cuisinart utensils of late.

This is a set of 7 tools though I say that begrudgingly. There are 4 actual utensils – a knife, a spatula, a scraper and a fork. Also included are a knife sheath and two squirt bottles for oil and/or sauces.

It looks like a nice set, but it isn’t anything special. The problem is in the quality, or rather the lack of it. The metal is thin and soft, so it is very easy to bend the fork without trying too hard. I spatula is also flexible and I worry that if I try to lift something with any weight the spatula will bend. The knife isn’t high end either, being comparable to a store-brand generic.

The handles aren’t much better. They’re real wood, but they feel cheap and I do not expect them to last.

I wouldn’t call this a bad set. It does what it’s supposed to do and it’s a decent starter set, but I would not recommend it to people who are looking for a set for more advanced/skilled cooks or are looking for a high-quality set for frequent, heavy use.

The truth about this percolator. Visually this percolator looks virtually identical to the original Farberwares from the 1950's that were made in the USA.  The new units being sold today are manufactured in China. The base and handle are made of dense heat resistant plastic that emulates the phenolic material used in the original models. The result is a slightly lighter pot. The finish on the metal is less resilient than found on the older models and somewhat more susceptible to discoloration. This won't be an issue if you care for the pot properly and keep it clean. The brew cycle is quite fast which some people will like. The downside to a quick brewing cycle is much less yield from your coffee grinds.  It takes at least 3 standard scoops to yield 4 cups of medium strength coffee. That's about 50% less efficient than what a decent drip machine will deliver. On the upside, the quick brewing cycle doesn't overcook the coffee and yields pretty decent results. The Achilles heel on these machines appears to be the heating element. If you get a good unit you can expect 3 or 4 years out of this pot with regular use, perhaps a bit more if you're lucky. That said there seems to be a fair number of these units that suffer from premature heating element failure. The elements are either made cheaply, not big enough, or not always installed properly.  That said you'll be hard pressed to find a nicer looking retro styled pot that makes decent percolated coffee for $50. No, it's not the same as the virtually indestructible Farberware pots from the 50's and 60's but it's a pretty decent product all things considered. Purchase an inexpensive Square Trade or similar extended warranty on it for a few bucks for peace of mind and you won't have to worry if you end up with a bad one.

It was used in a spare bedroom that’s been used less than 10 times so it’s been washed less than 10 times and the seams are coming apart. I reached out to the company and they fixed the issue but because of the issue with the product I still won’t give 5 stars.
Make this lite like a painting than a photocopy on canvas. While I love this artwork and still have it on my wall, this looks more like a colored photocopy than a replica of a painting.

Nice topper - be sure to note the back is flat.. This was a lovely tree topper, I just expected a little more. I think it's important to note that the back of this is more or less flat, so if you are thinking you are getting a starburst effect - the silver part just sorts of sticks out behind all the star. It looks nice, but i think my expectations were a bit higher.

Looks nice, but the price is steep for only one side.. I'm a huge potter fan and really wanted this for my office. I thought the price tag was a bit high -- but decided to order it instead. It's important to note, THIS IS ONLY ONE PIECE, so if you are not leaning the other side against a wall or something sturdy, you'll need to buy some other sort of bookend to keep it up. At the end of the day, I didn't like that one end looked all nice Potterish and the other end was just blah - especially for the price. For that price, it should have two pieces.

It works thus far. Feels a bit flimsy.. These definitely get the job done. They feel a bit flimsy, but are holding up so far. I use them for flats, sandals and other lightweight shoes. I will make one note -- read the instructions! It's easy to put the part that has the hangar in upside down and it pokes through/rips the fabric if you do, make sure it's in the right way.

Seems to work.... Honestly - not sure I noticed a difference. I mean I guess the Keurig seems cleaner, but the coffee doesn't taste different, so perhaps that's an A+ rating for the product right there.

Cute Confetti, small bag.. The confetti was nice, but please be warned that this is one small bag of confetti. For some reason, I thought there would be more to it than the price. It was enough to scatter on about 4 round tables sparingly.

It's a beautiful throw but.... ...the colors that are shown aren't true IRL. I got the green which had shown more of a lighter, sage green but when it came it was a darker Kelly green. Still, it's a beautiful throw it was just too dark for what I bought it for. If there were more color options I'd consider getting another color for myself as it was a nice throw.

Too tightly rolled. So....I couldn't use this yet because it was too tightly rolled up. I now have to train it to be flat as the edges keep curling treating to kill everyone as they trip on said rolled edges.
Its very pretty though so fingers crossed for next year!

Pretty pricey for the quality. I guess from the other reviews I was expecting something different. While these are nice they aren't exactly 'finest quality'. The pairs I received had a very rough feeling at the end where it would go in your mouth. I'm not a fan of splinters on my tongue. The box is nice but impractical for storage. I have had other laminated wood chopsticks that were better quality. They did clean easy but that isn't surprising with the lacquer finish.

Nothing to write home about. This is the second comforter ordered. The first exceeded ever expectation and I was so thrilled, I got new second for my bed, this time a king. Well...I want to know who measured this. It is the same size as my queen sized. I have a large queen bed which is why I ordered a king. I wake to no covers because it slipped off the bed as it is too short. It's a decent spring/fall comforter for here in the South where it rarely gets too cold.

Product needs work.. Difficult to use the different parts to this product. The blades stick--which is really challenging when you are trying to change them out and don't want to slice a finger! Blades are very sharp and when you finally get everything in place, it works great.
Too sharp!. These are too slick with varnish and too pointed to use for meals for this American! They are Korean styled, rather than the Chinese I am used to using!

... and awkwardly shaped for pictures--I thought it would work better, but this is probably only good for picturing .... Too small and awkwardly shaped for pictures--I thought it would work better, but this is probably only good for picturing one or maybe two people in it.

Not what I was hoping for. Not a big fan of this. Bought it for cooking French fries and fried chicken. Fries worked well (although a little soggy so I had to take them out, pat them dry, and refry them for a bit. I had also hoped I could do the chicken, but this unit is too small. I mean, I was able to squeeze one nicely sized breast in here, but I found it ended up burning/over cooking the outside and after25 minutes was still pink on the inside (so I ended up finishing the chicken in the oven (ala shake and bake style). Anyway, if you are looking for something small, to do something small, this may be for you. It is cute and looks well made. However, there are no adjustments to the temperature (one temp fits all).

Nice litte steamer with flaws. I was excited when I saw this in the Vine newsletter. I was traveling to Florida last weekend and wanted a travel steamer to take with me for the trip. For pros, this is complact and attractive and does create steam (although not consistently. I am rating this as three stars because it had a propensity to leak (thank goodness I wasn't using this on silk). I was disappointed to say the least and although it did the trick on the few pants and shirts I had, I had them spotted with water (but fortunately did not stain anything when it dried).

Not impressed. For the plus side, this blender looks wonderful in my stainless steel kitchen. For the negative side, too expensive, too noisy, cheap plastic lid, doesn't work as well as my other Oster blender which is less than half the cost. If you are looking for something sleek and modern and beautiful to look at this is it. It does blend ok, but as I mentioned not like my cheaper blender. Look elsewhere.

Yes, it's a grater, but not something I normally would use. I want to start by declaring that I am an avid chef having attended several weeks worth of cooking courses in the Tuscany region of Italy over the past few years. Having said that, I have been used to having a hand-held grater to do much of my grating of lemons, cheese, vegetables etc. It was something I picked up in Italy at a flea market for a few dollars similar to this style: [[ASIN:B004VLYQGS OXO Good Grips Fine Zester/Grater]].

This was my first time in using a box style grater. First, I found it bulky and difficult to manipulate (especially with trying to grate cheese). I also found clean up to be a little more difficult (not as easy to maneuver to the reverse side espcially when trying to use this with lemon rinds). I found myself scratching the back of my hand inside while trying to reach into all the nooks and crannys). I gave this 3 stars only because the product is well made, attractive and might be a style that someone may be looking for. It's just not something I will be using again. Give me the hand-held style any day.

A good entry level set for the new bride. Let's start with the pros: this is a large set with almost every kind of knife you could need (and even scissors), it's attractive and professional to look at on the countertop. Here are the cons: set is poorly made and the knives get marks/discolorations on them after several runs through the diswasher, handles feel loose and almost wobbly when using them for chopping, they only remain sharp for a short period of time (I found myself sharpening them after only two uses of dicing vegetables. I think this is a great entry level set for a bride-to-be and would look great as a relatively inexpensive shower present. However, if you are a serious cook (such as I consider myself to be) save your money and invest in a good steak knife set (which will cost over $200). It's like they say, you get what you pay for. It's attractive, but not functional.

Good memory foam pillow - average in performance. I am a side sleeper and typically buy pillows from Macys which are relatively high priced for my support and needs ($100+). When I saw this pillow in Vine I snatched it up thinking it could be a good, lower-priced alternative for me. I will say that the support is decent, but not like the higher priced pillows I am used to purchasing. I also don't really understand the purpose of the shape and find it a tad awkward, particularly when trying to put it in a pillow case. Anyway, it is good as a pillow but I don't think if I had to buy it I would. I have since stopped using it and have placed it in the linen closet figure it will be good for an extra pillow if I need one. A little disappointed, but overall it held it's shape and did give support. I wouldn't recommend it for heavy duty side sleepers. I guess you get what you pay for.

So-so Espresso machine. Not knowing what the price will be on this Espresso machine by Singolo makes it difficult to accurately review it. If it goes for less than $100, it may be worth the money (but I think this is unlikely). Positives: coffee comes out great and the unit is easy to use. Negatives: this machine is huge (heightwise)and makes it difficult to find a place to keep out on my countertop (I actually had to store it in my hall closet). I also have a Delonghi Espresso Machine, which I purchased on Amazon, that I really prefer to the Singolo. And, as the other reviewer had stated, it is disappointing to find that this unit is actually made in China (and not Italy).

You get what you pay for. These are attractive looking glasses, don't look like plastic from afar. I was disappointed in the weight and feel of them. Almost like they are less weight than a Solo plastic cup. Not sure if I would ever use these for company, unless we are using them outside. I think buying disposable ones at the supermarket would work just as well.

Hardly any fragrance, short burn time, didn't like. I was very disappointed with this candle. First, I burn candles all the time in my home (even leave a small tea light scented on in my bathroom when I am home for hours each day. When I saw this candle, I was really interested to try it as I have used Via Mercato items before (I love their liquid soaps) and I really like them. I won't go into too much detail here because many others have expressed the concerns I have. First, it's the amount of time you can burn this (one hour) is totally ridiculous. Second, I also don't like the way this burns (down the center). And last, but more importantly is the fragrance, there is barely any to discern (I had the Peach and Fig variety). Very disappointed and won't be buying again.

180 snowflakes. 9 Sheet Halloween window clings. Quality Jute charger squares not napkins !!. These are just ok for what they are and took longer than expected to arrive.
