Tough on garlic, easy on arthritic hands. As someone who frequently cooks Mediterranean menus heavy on fresh garlic, the Oxo garlic press is a chef's best friend. Rubber-coated handles make gripping and squeezing more user friendly than all-metal garlic presses, and cleanup is a snap. Like most garlic presses, you can choose to pre-peel the garlic before pressing it, but you'll still need to clean the press in-between uses. It comes with a built-in cleaner, and usually a quick run under the tap will remove most debris. The garlic comes out as more of a paste than it would if you were to chop it, and is a much faster way to add flavor to soups, salads, and more with minimal effort.

I've owned my Oxo press for years and haven't had any of the problems that other reviewers mentioned (handles falling off, hinge breaking). I do usually hand-wash, and I don't prepeel my garlic, and the press is still going strong 2+ years later. Perhaps my press was subject to different quality control standards: I bought it several years ago and had it stored until recently.

This sifter is a lifesaver on arthritic hands!. As someone who a) does a lot of baking and b) has had arthritis for the past two decades, Oxo's Good Grips Sifter is a lifesaver for sore hands. Instead of the usual squeeze trigger found on metal sifters, the Oxo sifter swings from side to side, no squeezing required.

In addition to the user-friendly design, the Oxo can measure up to two cups of flour, and the included top and bottom storage lids add to its versatility. This is a wonderful gift for any cook.

A lifesaver for those on the go.... As a grad student with a more-than-hectic schedule, I usually roll out of bed and run out the door. This Brew 'n Go Personal Coffeemaker and Travel Mug have saved the day! Water heats extremely rapidly and it takes no more than 2 minutes from turning the unit on until my coffee/tea is ready.

I use it to heat water for tea more often than I use it for coffee, and I've found that I have to let the tea steep a little longer than if I'd boiled the water on the stove, but it's still extremely convenient and easy to use.

The 15-oz. travel mug retains heat well and has a rubber-coated handle and nonskid bottom, which is a nice feature. The coffeemaker can be used with a permanent filter or paper filters (I prefer using disposable unbleached paper filters to the wire basket filter, as it can be messy to clean from the coffee bean oil accumulations). The coffeemaker shuts off automatically after brewing, another nice feature for those on the go (and one less thing to worry about on the way to work).

My only complaint would be that the plastic-coated inside of the travel mug is scratched up from using spoons to stir in sugar.

Overall, a good value for a rapid, portable mug of joe. For those who are coffee junkies, this will save you hundreds of dollars over buying your morning coffee fix from Starbucks, Beaners or Second Cup.

A big step up from bargain toasters.... I spent years in graduate school making do with a five-dollar toaster. After moving into my first home, I decided it was definitely worth the splurge to upgrade to a toaster worthy of my homemade breads. I was given a KitchenAid 2-Slice Toaster as a housewarming gift, and the love affair hasn't stopped since.

The KitchenAid performs all the usual functions of a toaster, with many choices from light to dark, but also features a bagel setting designed to toast the cut side of bagels more thoroughly than the crust, and a "warm" setting to keep your toast warm without turning it into charcoal.

The toaster has a nice solid construction, with heavy-duty metal parts and a well-built crumb tray that slides out, eliminating the mess from trapdoor-style crumb trays found on cheaper toasters.

Since I bake my own bread, I tend to slice it thickly, and it turns out perfectly in the KitchenAid. But beware: if you use store-bought (or other thinly sliced) breads, the extra-wide slots mean that your toast may turn out very light and need an extra toasting since the bread is held further away from the heating elements. But it performs beautifully on bagels, English muffins, and thick slices of bread. Whoever said that man cannot live by bread alone failed to toast it in a KitchenAid toaster!

Pros
Toasts evenly, bagels come out perfectly done

Cons
Sometimes frozen breads require extra toasting, warming feature ineffective

My Krups Power XL6 is my new best friend and favourite toy.. I received it as a surprise gift this past holiday season, and I am completely impressed. My Krups XL6 Combi blender came with a food processor attachment, making it even more versatile. The real reason I wanted a blender was for ice crushing and smoothie making, and after reading scores of negative reviews for other blenders regarding broken blades and fried motors after ice crushing, I was a little nervous to try it out. For the trial run I put in seven large ice cubes, put the lid on, and cautiously pushed the ice crusher button. This thing has the power of a jackhammer disguised as a blender! My ice was a perfect slushy consistency in seconds, with no large chunks of ice stuck under the blades (I've had that happen more than once). Two other nice features are that there is a removable measuring cup in the blender lid, which makes it handy for mixing alcoholic beverages (I've tried both daiquiris and piña coladas and both turned out superbly with minimum fuss and cleanup), and that the blender jar holds over a liter and half (50 oz.). There are 14 speeds, although I'm still in love with ice crushing for the moment, and the instruction manual covers chopping nuts, herbs, cheeses, instructions for milkshakes, purées, guacamole and more. The only downside was that the blade assembly with seal is made from plastic, and I couldn't remove it for fear of breaking it, so I wash it and dry it still in-jar. And the cord is a little on the short side. But these are only minor gripes, and overall I'm extremely pleased.

Reinventing the measuring cup. I have arthritis in my knees, and find it difficult to continually stoop over to read the measurements on liquid measuring cups. No more! Oxo Angled Measuring Cups features easy-to-read measurements (the cups also feature metric equivalents) that can be viewed from above. This set of three measuring cups (1, 2, and 4 cups) is an excellent value and makes a thoughtful housewarming / wedding present (but be sure to buy a set for yourself as well).

It takes a little practice to pour and read accordingly, but once you have the hang of it, you'll never go back to old-fashioned measuring cups that require stooping and bending.

My best friend for microwave cooking!. My college roommate bought the Joyce Chen Microwave Rice Steamer for me as a birthday present, and it's easily one of my most-used tools in the kitchen. It can be used for a variety of dishes, from rice to couscous, popcorn, and steamed veggies. I've tried several varieties of rice (short, medium, and long grain) and couscous, air-popped popcorn (no oil added), and various veggies (broccoli, cauliflower, asparagus), and everything comes out perfectly. Simply add water, slip in the steamer tray (if cooking veggies) and the two lids (one to lock in steam), and in a few minutes, you'll have a healthy, fast option for lunches and dinners. I hand wash mine, but you could probably put it in the dishwasher on the top rack. Simple to use and easy to clean, every kitchen should have one of these!

Authentic Italian espresso at an affordable price. After many happy (and dare I say, naive) years with our DeLonghi Caffe Espresso, it was time to replace our old workhorse. Having just spent the summer in Spain, where no bar is complete without the standard superautomatic Gaggia espresso maker, I decided that truly great espresso was a daily necessity. I was tired of incompetent teenagers / college students who work at local coffee shops mangling something as simple as a cappuccino (one part espresso, one part milk, one part foam) into a milk-drowned latte with no foam.

I wanted something in the range of $200, with a dependable track record and plenty of power to spare. I waded through a myriad of reviews for the Gaggia Carezza, hailed as a champion of its class, but read a number of negative reviews concerning design shortcomings.

Enter the Gaggia Evolution. Although the Gaggia Carezza and Evolution share the same innards, the Evolution boasts several improvements in design. With its 17.5 bar pump and high wattage, dual element boiler, the Gaggia Evolution is ready to brew in around 5-10 minutes (I always prime the boiler first).

Design improvements over the Carezza include: a larger drip tray, a cup warmer (although, as usual, it's more effective to preheat your cups by filling them with hot water, which can be done during priming), anti-vibration mounts (once primed, the Gaggia Evolution is nearly whisper-quiet), and a brass commercial portafilter (the spouts on the Carezza were changed to plastic). My Evolution came with the Perfect Crema device (which is supposed to go under the single filter basket in order to create additional pressure/allow a coarser grind), but having read numerous negative reviews of the ineffective device, I simply left it in the box with the packing material.

Five stars for the instruction manuals and CD-ROM: the Gaggia Evolution comes with not one, but two instruction manuals: one from the manufacturer (Gaggia), and one from the North American importer (Importika). The Importika manual is intuitive, easy to read and injected with coffee humor, although the Evolution is not among the Gaggia models listed in the Appendix. The included CD-ROM walks you through setup in the form of short movies and narration, along with more advanced tips and techniques for coffee connoisseurs. We put our laptop on the kitchen table and followed along after unpacking our new Gaggia (thankfully, nothing was broken in the mail, as happened to several Gaggia Carezza owners). Although the manual hinted that your first coffee might not be potable, we'd followed various tips online (prime your new machine several times to remove any residue and plastic-y taste), and our first espresso was laden with crema. The Turbo Frother attachment made the creamiest, densest microfoam I have ever seen-it looked more like meringue (hint: use skim milk for best results). My only complaint would be the cheapness of the included coffee scoop, and you definitely want to invest in a better tamp for maximum extraction (the Gaggia takes a 58 mm tamp at a recommended 30 pounds of pressure).

If you're not in the market to buy a $200-300 grinder (Rancilio Rocky or Gaggia 8002 MDF Burr Grinder) to go with your new Gaggia, Illy makes a delicious, dependable espresso grind, available in tins (decaf, too) or Pods. The Evolution is Pod-ready, simply use the single shot basket with the portafilter. Tip: "classic" double shots should take around 20-25 seconds to extract.

The Evolution is a steal for the current price, since it contains the same innards as other Gaggias in the $400-500 range. Although it runs around $50-100 more than the Carezza, I appreciated the design improvements, stylish lines (I have a Tuscan kitchen with hand-painted ceramics and terra cotta tiles and was afraid that the "modern" styling would stand out, but the Evolution is much more traditional-looking and unobtrusive than the Carezza), and performance. (Note: the Evolution is also available in an all-silver model, but it will set you back another $50. The black model features a black base and sides and a silver front and silver drip tray.)

Excellent for the espresso novice or connoisseur, easy to use and clean, and it makes better espresso than some $500-1,000 machines I've tried!

Easy to use and an impressive presentation. This mini Bundt Cake Pan features six one-cup cakes in three different designs based on classic Bundt pans. Although much smaller than their full-size counterparts, there is still an astonishing amount of detail, making these perfect for elegant individual desserts. For optimum "wow" factor, try dusting chocolate cakes with a light dusting of confectioner's sugar to bring out the details.

The included instructions say to use unsalted vegetable shortening or spray, but I used my ubiquitous Baker's Joy and had no problems unmolding the cakes from the pan (try shaking the pan gently side-to-side and front-to-back before unmolding for easier removal). Also, if you fill the molds the typical 2/3 full, you will probably have a couple of cups or so of batter left over from a recipe scaled for a 10-cup Bundt pan. The pan is a dream to clean and washes easily with hot soapy water (I refrained from using a nylon scrubber on the non-stick coating).

Perfect for special occasions, elegant romantic dinners, and individual easy-to-serve portions for office parties, this mini Bundt Pan from Nordic Ware is another solid performer from a company with a long tradition of excellent product performance and durability.

Absolutely gorgeous presentation. Nordic Ware's Violet Bundt Pan makes an absolutely stunning presentation; criss-crossed with tendrils and ringed with a base of raised-detail violet leaves, the top of the cake is sprinkled with a ring of raised violets. The details show off particularly well when using unglazed cakes (a dusting of powdered sugar on darker cakes or a dusting of cocoa on lighter cakes will bring out the details). This is always a showstopper when I make my signature Mexican Fudge Pecan Cake from [[ASIN:1580085628 The Pastry Queen: Royally Good Recipes from the Texas Hill Country's Rather Sweet Bakery & Cafe]], and people always think that my cakes made in the Violet Bundt came from some upscale bakery. Pricey, but it's made in the USA and will be a faithful friend for years.

Vive La France!. I discovered these gems while staying at the excellent Inn at Grey Gables in Charlevoix, MI. Inspired by the Napoleonic bee, these sturdy French tumblers from La Rochere are crafted in France from crystal-clear glass. They have a hefty weight in the hand, with thick bottoms that prevent toppling over. They are perfect for fresh-squeezed orange juice and make a dramatic presentation on your table at breakfast or anytime. Although stated to be dishwasher-safe, I hand-wash mine to prevent etching. These unique heavy-duty French tumblers will last a lifetime with care and are sure to add French flair to your home.

Easy to make, easy to clean, and they look professional!. I bought the Nordicware Sweetheart Rose Muffin/Cake pan since I bake a lot of muffins and wanted a more "professional" appearance. Instead of boring, bland muffins, the Nordicware Sweetheart Rose pan makes 12 1/2 cup roses in intricate detail, including rosebuds and leaves. I use Baker's Joy to grease the pan before baking, and add a light dusting of confectioner's sugar to the finished muffins / cakes so as not to cover up the details. Cleaning is a snap: normally, there is no batter left in the pans, ever with all the nooks and crannies. The pan is also a good solid weight, something sorely missing in all those "made in China" knock-offs (Nordicware is still made in the USA). This is an easy, beautiful presentation for teacakes, muffins, and cupcakes that look like you bought them at a bakery.

Pricey, but effective. For years, I'd struggled with heaving pots of boiling water to the sink and attempting to dump the contents into a colander, where the backwash of hot water would inevitably flood whatever I was cooking and end up splashing me in the process. Last year I ended up purchasing the Oxo convertible colander, which is a lifesaver (that, and buy a pasta pot). It has foldable legs that extend to fit over the edges of your sink, holding the colander in place so you can keep both hands on the pot of boiling water. The holes wrap around the sides and the bottom, so your contents drain evenly. When you're finished, the legs simply fold down and you can slide the colander onto a shelf for easy storage (it's also a great place to stash frequently used baking / cook's tools such as mini pastry rollers and tartlette pans). This is definitely one of the handiest, best-designed kitchen tools I own.

The perfect housewarming gift. This 7-piece utensil set with enameled stoneware crock is a perfect housewarming gift or a great starter investment for students heading off to college. To be honest, I mostly wanted the set for the utensil crock, as I have searched unsuccessfully for one large enough and sturdy enough to hold my everyday whisks and spatulas, and the Le Creuset stoneware crock is large enough to double as a makeshift vase or wine cooler (the stoneware cools down quickly) in a pinch. The utensils are extraordinarily handy, particularly if you're always having to hunt for a spatula (or can't find one that's the right size). They're perfect for nonstick cookware, and withstand up to 800-degree heat. The silicone heads are detachable for (fairly) easy cleaning. The only thing that would have made this set perfect was the inclusion of a silicone whisk, a necessity for stirring sauces and liquid ingredients in nonstick saucepans. Otherwise, this is a great value, and you're sure to get years of use from the included spatulas.

Fiestaware withstands the test of time. My grandmother had a set of blue Fiestaware mixing bowls, so in a way, I grew up with the bright colors, durability and classic styling of Homer Laughlin's signature line. Recently, I moved into my first home and was given a set of four heather four-piece place settings. I plan to add on to the collection as more pieces are added in the newest color, heather.

This four-piece set comes with a dinner plate, salad plate, stackable cereal bowls, and a mug in place of the teacup and saucer present in the five-piece place setting. Besides being durable (it's dishwasher, microwave, and oven-safe), lead-free, and coming with a 3-year chip warranty, Fiestaware has been made in the USA since 1936.

The classic Art Deco styling and wide range of coordinates (vases, teapots, trays, candlesticks, spoon rests, salt and pepper shakers) means that it?s fabulously easy to mix and match various colors for an eye-catching effect. The dishes are substantial in weight, and make a striking presentation for any meal. Fiestaware is an excellent investment and the perfect wedding or housewarming gift.

A lifesaver for a small kitchen!. My kitchen is very small and has very limited counter space, so I have a problem when I bake several sheets of cookies. Enter the Baker's Mate, which holds up to four cookie sheets. It is very sturdy and doesn't take up much counter space, allowing you to stack four cookie sheets at a time in a relatively small area (unlike trying to find room for four cooling racks!). It folds up for easy storage and is made in Sweden.

Makes your holiday table shine. I purchased the Lenox "Holiday Nouveau" 70" round tablecloth to coordinate with several Lenox Holiday Nouveau serving pieces. Crafted of 58% cotton, 42% polyester and machine-washable (cold water with like colors), the ivory-on-ivory holly leaves catch the light and make the tablecloth shimmer, while the tartan ribbon is accented with holly and berries. Be sure to pick up the matching napkins for a gorgeous presentation!

Keeps your butter cool, fresh, and ready to spread. Emile Henry Auberge butter pots are the perfect addition to your breakfast table or afternoon tea. This glazed ceramic crock is a time-tested design, and keeps your butter fresh, cool and spreadable thanks to a reservoir of cold water that you replenish every few days (the water creates an airtight seal). It holds 8 oz. (one cup) of butter, plenty to satisfy the whole family at mealtimes. No more rock-hard pats of butter when your toast or rolls are ready! Plus, this new color (figue) coordinates beautifully with Fiestaware's heather dishes.

A convenient way to bake and store your favorite pies. The Pyrex Pie Plate Portable combines the classic 9" Pyrex pie plate with a sturdy plastic carrier (the plastic bottom locks into the lid). This makes it an ideal way to transport your homemade pies (or quiches) to office functions and parties without fighting with cling wrap or foil. The saucer-shaped bottom part of the carrier keeps the pie plate from sliding around, preserving your crust. The lid also has several small holes that avoid moisture from collecting inside the lid, which is particularly handy if your pie is still slightly warm. I stored my bourbon chocolate pecan pie inside the fridge, and the crust held up fine after several days inside the carrier. The handle is fairly sturdy, and it's easy to twist the lid open and closed (a blessing on arthritic hands!). Naturally, the pie carrier isn't oven-safe, so it's best to let your pie cool completely before loading it into the carrier.  Best of all, it's made in the USA. This would make a great housewarming (or wedding shower) gift.

A clever multitasker with easy cleanup...just don't go by the manual!. I've owned several George Foreman grills over the years, so I was thrilled that I had the chance to test out the Smart Kitchen Multicooker. My regular workhorse [[ASIN:B0007VZZNO Black & Decker HS1000 Handy Steamer with Flavor Scenter Screen]] was getting on in years, and was limited to steaming. However, the George Foreman Multicooker has a 5-quart capacity, and you can sear directly in the pan, then add your other ingredients to make stews, sauces, stir-fry, etc. Like the George Foreman grills, the nonstick coating allows for less oil or butter in cooking, cutting down on fat. There's also an adjustable steam vent on the lid. You can cook two things at once; for example, you can cook rice in the main pot while putting shrimp, fish, veggies, etc in the steamer basket above the rice, not only saving time but cutting down on dishes as well.

As other reviewers have mentioned, don't count on the included "instruction" manual for much guidance. In fact, if you relied on the manual alone, you probably wouldn't have much of a feel for the versatility of the product. It's a great help to watch the promo video on the official George Foreman website (see my post below for the URL). One thing I would have liked to have seen was a comprehensive list of steaming times for various ingredients similar to the manual from my old Black and Decker steamer (it included separate guides for meat, fish, veggies, frozen vs. fresh, etc.), although the Intelli-Probe digital controls have presets for rice and other settings. Another minus is the fittings for the steamer basket handles; these were roughly finished (it looked like the ends were clipped, resulted in sharp, uneven surfaces), and with frequent use I could see them scratching the nonstick coating of the pan.

Overall, this is a handy tool to have around the kitchen if you frequently cook large quantities of food since it has a 20-cup capacity, and being able to sear in the same pan is a great feature. However, the lack of suggested cooking times makes it a bit more difficult to use than a regular steamer.

if you are expecting the taste and texture of regular tofu, you will be sorely disappointed !!. To all the people unfairly bashing this item giving it one star, that is exactly what  Koyadofu  supposed to look/feel/taste like… You cannot use this the same as regular tofu, you have to rehydrate it, then simmer it with dashi and seasonings.  It is an Integral part of our Shojin Ryori, or temple cuisine here in Japan.  Named after the sacred Mt Koya,  this is a unique preparation to enjoy tofu and the sponge like texture it makes it a great meat substitute  when crumbled in hamburgers, mapo dofu, etc.  it seems a bit unfair so many people have given this item a bad rap when that is no fault of the manufacture, it is more of the unfamiliarity with the product.

Stops spills, but the design could use some improving. I first saw the Kuhn Rikon Kochblume at Sur La Table, and was intrigued. One of the messiest things to clean up is a pot that's boiled over, so I was interested to see if it would work.

I read other reviews and followed the following tips, and it worked as advertised:

* First, this is made for pots with a diameter of 5.5 - 9". Any larger, and the spill stopper will slide into the pot / not catch overflow that extends beyond the diameter of the pot!!

* Two words: steam burns. Other reviewers advise not checking the pasta for doneness, as there is a LOT of steam built up under the spill stopper, which forms a seal to keep water from boiling out. Also, if you lift the spill stopper to test for doneness, there's the potential to dump starch and boiling water all over the stovetop. I also don't recommend lifting up only one side to check; again, steam burns, ouch! Common sense applies: don't lean directly over the pot when removing the spill stopper to check / drain pasta.

I tried boiling a LOT of dried pasta in a small pot to see if I could get it to boil over: nope. The foam bubbled up through the petals and crept for several inches beyond the pot's edges (still several inches away from the edge of the silicone) but the sturdy silicone prevented the foam from running over or water to escape between the edge of the pot and the spill stopper.

The little "flower" in the center is held in place by a plastic clip; it can be removed for cleaning or to create a splatter shield according to the package directions. My only complaint here is that the "petals" are very thin, flimsy silicone that would be easy to accidentally rip (and these are what keep the starchy foam from overflowing). Some reviewers have had the petals rip off and bond with glass, so I would wash the spill stopper separately. The starchy buildup can also be a pain to remove; thank goodness it's dishwasher safe!

Verdict: Yes, it works. Definitely invest in the large, which fits 5.5-9" diameter pots (including my Italian pasta pot).

(See photo above for a pic of the spill stopper in action; I loaded my 2QT pot with a good 5 oz. of dried pasta and 1QT of water to see what would happen!)

Great addition to USA Pan's nonstick bakeware lineup - made in USA too!. I own numerous pans by USA Pan... in fact, it's the only brand I bake with. From muffin pans to jelly roll pans to cookie sheets, sheet pans and specialty pans, USA Pan is my brand of choice due to its durability, ease of cleaning, and best of all, the fact that it's manufactured in the USA (an increasing rarity these days).

In the past, I baked with a stoneware pizza pan that was made in PRC...I try to buy American (or European) whenever possible, as I don't trust the materials being used as I've had several bad experiences in the past with substandard products / defective coatings, etc.

So when I was offered the chance to try out the USA Pan pizza stone, I was thrilled to find a made-in-the-US alternative for my homemade pizza crusts and rustic breads.

First of all, this pan is LARGE - so for those of you with smaller countertop convection ovens, this will be too large to fit. It has a wonderfully solid feel and heft. Made from clay mined in Tennessee, best of all, the pizza stone features the same nonstick finish used on their metal bakeware, meaning that you will no longer be scrubbing off the seared-on pizza cheese or drips that plague regular stoneware. It comes with a 3-year warranty.

Because this item is stoneware, never place a warm pan in cold water to reduce risk of breaking. Due to the nonstick finish, avoid steel wool or abrasive cleaners. Also, do NOT preheat and do not exceed 450. By following these tips, your USA Pizza Stone should give you many years of faithful use.

Fewer bells and whistles than the made-in-Germany models; does a satisfactory job, especially on cotton items. I used a Rowenta Advancer DZ9080 iron for years and was very pleased with it. Recently I switched to the Rowenta Autosteam DW4060. The Autosteam model is a lower-end Rowenta product made in China. It does not have all the features of the more expensive Rowentas made in Germany but it does a satisfactory job. I enjoy ironing so have it given the Autosteam a thorough trial. I have been very pleased with the result on cotton items.

The DW4060 has several features that make ironing a bit less stressful. The iron has a scratch-resistant Airglide stainless steel soleplate which results in a smooth non-stick glide across fabrics. In addition, the burst of steam option helps removes those stubborn wrinkles. One of the most helpful features is the precision tip for precise ironing down to the smallest detail.

My only complaint with this iron is that I found it difficult to determine the water level in the reservoir. Several times I overfilled and ended up with a wet ironing board cover.

) Like other USA Pans. USA Pan is the only brand I bake with; I own numerous starter sets and specialty pans, so I was thrilled to see they now make a 9-inch springform pan (Useful not only for cheesecakes, but any kind of molded desserts, stuffed pies, etc. )

Like other USA Pans, this one is coated with a special nonstick coating that ensures your baked goods will release easily. The heavy weight means heat diffuses and bakes evenly. Note that this pan is a bit larger / heavier that standard springform pans, so if you have a smaller countertop oven, that's something to consider. The bottom tray on the pan also sticks out quite a bit more than other springform pans I have.

Like my other USA Pans, I was thrilled with the performance; I have not tried using this in a water bath yet (my oven is too small to fit a roasting pan in), but for non-water-bath baked goods, the oversized tray catches all drips / overflows.

Worked like a charm!. I frequently make cheesecakes and the occasional flourless cake, so I was looking forward to testing out the Kuhn Rikon PushPan. I followed the included instructions and used it to bake the chocolate almond torte from [[ASIN:1455617466 Scandinavian Classic Desserts (Classics)]]. As I was making it for a gluten-free / Passover audience, I used butter to grease the pan instead of my usual Baker's Joy (which contains flour). I made sure to press the bottom in securely; because there is a fair amount of resistance from the silicone gasket, you'll want to press down firmly on a level surface to make sure you have the bottom in all the way.

I wrapped heavy-duty foil around the base of the pan just in case, but no liquid seeped out through the silicone gasket (although I haven't tried it with a really wet batter yet). Once the cake had baked, I cooled it fully on a rack before removing the sides, which was a snap! I placed the pan on a can of peanuts (make sure that whatever item you use to remove the sides is a) taller than the PushPan and b) stable!), pushed down gently, and my chocolate torte sprang free without any of the batter stuck to the sides of the PushPan. Because I'd also used a buttered parchment round, the cake slid easily off the bottom. The nonstick used on the pan appears to be heavy-duty, and cleanup was a snap.

Some reviewers have mentioned that the 9" PushPan is smaller than a conventional springform pan, so you may want to take that into consideration if you're making a good-sized cheesecake.

Bottom line: easy cleanup and operation make the PushPan a winner, although I'm not sure about the longevity of the silicone gasket; it looks like something that may require replacement if you use it a lot. It is also available in 8" and 10" sizes.

Worth it for the cherry blossom and rose stamps. I managed to land the [[ASIN:B00ABH0PYI OXO Good Grips Cookie Press with Disk Storage Case]] as a Vine item, and fell madly in love with it. I have an older Swedish metal cookie press that is built like a tank, but the trigger mechanism was hard on my arthritis. The OXO press, on the other hand, is as simple as loading the press with dough (the included booklet contains three base recipes for cream cheese, butter, and and chocolate shortbread spritz dough with several variations) and pressing down on the handle. I'd tried about six of the twelve included disks, but wanted something for spring (St. Pat's, Valentine's, etc.)

Enter the Springtime Disk Set, with gives you an additional six disks for your OXO cookie press: a cherry blossom, rose, LOVE stamp, two hearts, a shamrock, and a bouquet of flowers.

For St. Pat's, I made a double batch of green-tinted shamrocks with green sprinkles.

I'd specifically purchased this set for the cherry blossom stamp; as I have many Japan Air Self-Defense Force wingmen that I work with, I wanted to make up sakura (cherry blossom) cookie bags during hanami (cherry blossom viewing season). I ended up making a split batch of colored-and-sprinkled cherry blossoms and roses and packaging them in cellophane bags, and they were a hit! (see photo above) I used the OXO standard butter dough recipe that came with my press, although I've also tried the chocolate shortbread and lemon poppyseed variations, and they were also good (you can also find the recipes on the OXO website; see comments for the link).

One addition that would have been nice would have been an additional plastic storage case for the disks; the original storage case that came with [[ASIN:B00ABH0PYI OXO Good Grips Cookie Press with Disk Storage Case]] has slots for exactly 12 disks to keep them upright, and then I had to throw in the additional six disks from the Springtime set with no way to keep them from banging into the disks next to them.

A baking powerhouse with lots of great added features. The Breville 5-Quart Die-Cast Stand Mixer is my second stand mixer. I'm a heavy-duty home baker, so I need a durable stand mixer for creaming and whipping (I knead bread doughs by hand rather than in a stand mixer or food processor, which is the surest way to burn out a motor).

Setting up was a breeze. You simply push the button on top to tilt the mixer head, attach the desired attachment, lower the mixer head, and you're good to go. I appreciated that the mixer head has a very sturdy locking mechanism; there's no wobbling when you have the mixer head up to add / switch attachments. I also liked the handy "handle" on the front. Even with the mixer on medium-high, there was little movement of the unit.

I was thrilled that the Breville came with a scraper attachment; my first mixer was a Kitchen Aid, and I spent a sizable sum buying a nearly-identical attachment that wasn't included in the box. Just like with my Kitchen Aid, sliding and locking the various attachments is intuitive. There is also a dough hook, a wire whip, a metal flat beater, a rubber spatula and a pouring shield. I also liked the fact that the grounded plug is shaped like a doughnut; there's a hole in the middle so you can use one finger to pull out the plug if your hands are covered in flour, chocolate, etc. without getting the whole plug dirty.

Another feature I really liked was the ten-minute digital timer and the "pause" function (with my old KA mixer, you'd have to turn the mixer all the way off; a pause setting is really handy). And because the speed controls are digital (there are 12 speeds total), there's no grinding or sticking of gears (my mom went through *three* Kitchen Aid stand mixers under warranty due to stuck speed control levers and mixer gears).

This is an excellent choice for novices and pros alike.

Great for tile / wood floors, attachment tools could be better.... I needed something to vacuum up my tiled kitchen floor and linoleum bathroom floor, and the Electrolux Ergorapido fits the bill nicely. Setup was a breeze; the unit should be charged up to 24 hours before use. This 2-in-1 stick vac consists of a canister vac that snaps into the stick vac (the canister vac contains the filter). The storage base also holds a crevice tool and "dusting brush" (more on that in a moment). The Brushrollclean Technology allows the brush to self-clean, which is a great feature.

There are numerous features about the Electrolux that I really liked; the swivel head is great at reaching under the fridge and oven or along baseboards. I also liked that there are lights along the leading edge, so you can see if you've gotten everything. One off-putting thing was that upon the first several uses, both the canister vac and stic vac smelled strongly of Band-aids (must be from the plastic or components). I was also not crazy about the cheap feel of the charging cable cord, which seems brittle and lightweight. The charging stand and footprint are fairly small (you can also wall-mount the stand).

After using the stick vac in the kitchen and bathroom, next I tried using the canister vac in the car, and here is where I ran into problems with the attachment. I had an old Black and Decker canister vac that I used to use, and it had a brush that snapped directly onto the vacuum nozzle. The Electrolux requires that you first snap on the crevice tool (which is a good 8"-9") and then the brush; there is no way to attach the brush directly. Also, the dusting brush's bristles are MUCH softer than my old vac, so the bristles bent easily (I was using it to clean the leather seats). However, it did a good job at cleaning floormats and leather seats, so I'm happy. The reservoir holds a LOT, and the Electrolux definitely did a much better job at picking up dirt / debris than my old vacuum.

Overall there are many pluses for the Electorlux EL2021A; I loved the swivel head, the lights, the fact it is easy to store and maneuver (I can't comment on battery life as I've only used the vacuum for short runs so far). The two-year warranty was also a plus. My only critique is that I wished different tools were included, but otherwise it does a great job on tile / wood floors and as a hand vac.

Hummus among us!. I bought this to use as part of a photoshoot for a blog tour of [[ASIN:0425272230 My Fat Dad: A Memoir of Food, Love, and Family, with Recipes]] and wasn't disappointed. This was my first purchase of Mud Pie tableware, and I loved the embossed lettering (the spreader is made from a very lightweight metal and I would have preferred to see something more durable / weightier, but it gets the job done). The bowl is the perfect size for a single batch of hummus in the Vitamix using one can of chickpeas and makes a statement on your table! The only downside is the included spreader DOES leave faint grey marks on the glaze, so now I use a soft silicone spatula to clean out the bowl instead. This would make a super-cute housewarming gift or wedding gift paired with my friend Maureen Abood's hummus starter kit, available from Maureen Abood Market, as well as a copy of her excellent [[ASIN:0762454865 Rose Water and Orange Blossoms: Fresh & Classic Recipes from my Lebanese Kitchen]].

Blendtec Classic 575. For several years, I made do with a fairly inexpensive, retro-styled Oster blender...it did a decent (not great) job at blending (I frequently enlisted it to help with my award-winning San Antonio cajeta flan cake, which took second place at our first-ever squadron baking contest), however it was not so great at crushing ice for drinks.

Three years ago, I finally splurged and bought myself a Vitamix Pro Heritage 750. I was amazed at its ability to churn out smoothies, milkshakes, nut butters, flours, as well as piping hot soups. I loved the presets and the easy cleanup (add a drop or two of dishsoap and warm water just covering the blade assembly.).

My best friend is a manager at Bed Bath and Beyond and swore by her Blendtec. So when I had the opportunity to compare the Vitamix and Blendtec side by side, I was interested in putting the Blendtec through its paces.

The exterior on the unit I received is a white plastic that will fit in well with pretty much any decor. Also, Blendtecs have a digital control panel vs. the sliders / dials on older Vitamix Models, which took a little getting used to.

The 575 has four presets and the included instruction manual (which also has Spanish instructions) includes a few starter recipes.

Noise-wise, I found this a bit louder than the Vitamix due to the more powerful motor (1,575 watts). I liked that the blender blades are blunted compared to the "ninja star" design on most blenders that result in lacerations when cleaning / drying. Also, the Blendtec does not require a tamper due to the design of the WildSide blender jar (I appreciated the paper insert that illustrates the correct stacking order for ingredients!). It does a great job with smoothies (I haven't tried the other presets yet), no chunks of unblended ingredients and I love that it has an 8-year warranty and is made in the United States. (If you want to see it in action, there's a hilarious series of Blendtec promo videos called "Will it Blend?" where they put items like iPhones (don't try this at home!!) into a Blendtec and pulverize them...)

If you are looking to add a high-performance blender to your kitchen (and it is an investment that really does pay for itself!), you would do well to consider the Blendtec Classic 575 Blender.

Great durability + vintage design = classic Corelle!. Like many others, I grew up with several sets of Corelle dishes in my house, including pansies and the Christmas scene set, as well as coordinating bakers and accessories. So it was with no small sense of nostalgia (as well as a sense of pride that this line is still made in the USA) that I snapped these up (after moving into my own homes both stateside as well as overseas, the original set of Corelle is still in my childhood home). Oddly, these are not listed as Corelle plates, but most definitely are as they are marked on the back.

The weight and quality of these is on par with vintage Vitrelle glassware, and the decals are evenly placed (Corelle is dishwasher safe, but cannot be used in the oven or broiler). They are listed as chip and break resistant, and from long years of experience using Corelle (and dishwashing), it's quite likely the decals will eventually wear off, although the plates themselves are still serviceable 25+ years later. I also love that the manufacturing process uses 65% recycled glass. The packaging was very straightforward; all six plates were nestled into a slim cardboard box.

As a single household, this is the perfect-sized plate for me (I prefer serving meals on appetizer and salad plates as mealtimes largely involving mezze and grazing). They work well for serving appetizers, desserts, sandwiches, etc, and the retro print would be great fun for a potluck, mahjong gathering, or retro-themed party. These would also make a great gift for a new college student starting off on their own; I love the versatility, durability, and most of all, the fact that you can still find dishes made right here in the USA!

Handy Little Appliance to Have In The Kitchen. The Tiger 5 1/2 cup rice cooker has performed flawlessly on everything we've tried. Not only did it produce excellent results on various kinds of rice (white rice, brown rice, multigrain rice, wild rice) but it's also been good for cooking porridge (steel cut oats in our case) and even hard-boiled eggs). Nothing we've used it for has turned out less than perfect.

This cooker even has a synchro-cooking mode which allows you to cook concurrently using the included cook plate. I have not used this mode yet but have already picked out several fairly simple recipes which I plan to attempt in the near future.

Since cooking with a rice cooker is a new experience for me, I appreciated the Tiger operating instructions included with the unit. It is very thorough and contains helpful sections including basic how-to information and troubleshooting. Also included with this rice cooker is a cookbook which includes 25 recipes, many of which are for synchro-cooking. To help you explore the world of rice cooker cooking, I strongly recommend purchasing a basic rice cooker cookbook to accompany the included material. This will assist in unlocking the full potential of your rice cooker, a consistent and dependable option in preparing one-pot meals, side dishes, etc. You will find that the Tiger rice cooker is a surprisingly versatile addition to the kitchen, especially considering how little counter space it requires. It is easy to use and clean-up is easy, too.

If you have the time and patience, you could prepare many of the same things on your stove top that this rice cooker does, thereby saving the cost of purchasing one. The question to consider is whether the Tiger 5 1/2 cup rice cooker is worth its price in order to have the convenience of being able to set it to cook perfect rice while you do other things. That convenience is worth a lot to me, and I'm guessing to many other people as well.

Treats to go.. NordicWare has done it again with this covered aluminum muffin pan. This has been a lifesaver for me, since I used to take my muffins and cupcakes out of the pan, onto a cooling rack, and then into a separate container for work. By the time I got there, my cupcakes would have fallen over and smeared icing all over the place. No more!!

Perfect for muffins and cupcakes, the handy plastic storage lid means that you don't have to worry about squashed muffin tops or mangled icing (it also keeps muffins and cupcakes fresher longer). The aluminum pan promotes even browning, and with a quick spray of Baker's Joy (or cupcake liners), cleaning is a breeze. I've found that because this pan isn't nonstick, I do have to clean it more thoroughly, and that more batter sticks to the bottom of the cups. Also, the cups seem a bit shallower than a regular muffin pan. But the lid is a great feature that more than makes up for any shortcomings.

This gorgeous non-leaded crystal vase features varying shades of charcoal .... This gorgeous non-leaded crystal vase features varying shades of charcoal, amethyst, pearl, and clear and reminds me of an agate. Standing nearly a foot high, the dramatic swirls and graceful lines make a striking centerpiece for your table or entryway. I own numerous Lenox place settings, but this is my first experience with one of their vases. I'd been looking for something large enough to accommodate larger bouquets, and this fit the bill perfectly.

I liked the heavy construction. I own multiple digital scales that I use on a regular basis for baking, but this was my first OXO scale (although I own numerous OXO products).

Out of box, I liked the heavy construction. Included batteries were easy to install (I've had some scales that were nearly impossible to remove / access the battery compartment, so that's a plus). I like the feel of the glass top, and the ease of cleaning.

However, my least favorite feature is one of the selling points: the pull-out display. The construction of the lone wire/cable holding the digital display in place feels a little flimsy; I'm not opposed to a pull-out feature, but would have rather had something that slides out (mine ended up dangling off the edge of the counter as I had the scale at the very edge as I have very narrow counters and limited counter space).

Measurements seem accurate enough, although I would have liked a little more precision as I would occasionally weigh the same item twice and get slightly different readings. There is also no "tare" display to let you know the scale is in tare mode once hitting zero. Measurements include oz., fluid oz., pounds, grams, and mL.

As a battery saving feature, when you put the pull out display away, it seems to shut the unit off, which I liked. Also, the display stays on for a LONG time (maybe 5 minutes?), which is helpful when you're trying to prep, measure and weigh several items in a row without having to constantly reboot / tare the unit.

Overall, this will see a lot of use in my kitchen and I love the sturdy glass top and ease of cleaning. It is much thicker than my previous digital scale, but still slides neatly (or on its side) to take up little space.

Easy to use and dishwasher-safe. I use my Oxo 9" whisk for many different recipes (whipping air into eggs, mixing liquid ingredients, etc.), and it always performs like a pro and goes straight into the dishwasher for easy cleanup. My only recommendation would be to invest in a silicone-coated whisk as well; this will scratch up your nonstick cookware, but it works great for mixing and other general kitchen duties.

Great for saving money on iced coffee from major chains. Summers where I live are unbearably hot and humid, and I drink an ocean of cold brew and iced coffee. Sure, it's great to have the convenience of grabbing one from a major coffee chain, but that indulgence can quickly add up.

So I was happy to have the chance to try out the Asobu Portable Cold Brew Coffee Maker. It's a coldbrew maker and an insulated carafe all in once, which is nice. The build seems sturdy and mine has held up well. The design is very sleek as well, and the matte black finish is unobtrusive.

I keep my Asobu at my desk at work; you simply add any standard-grind drip coffee to the metal mesh filter, pour water over in a circular motion, and let steep. The mesh is fine enough prevent coffee granules from slipping through and falling into the coffee, which is nice. It's important to add the coffee grounds in stages; you add the first third, wet thoroughly, then continue to add grounds and water, finally pouring cold filtered water over the top.

When the coffee is finished brewing in 12-24 hours depending on how strong you like it (you can pop it into the fridge overnight), you simply press the button to drain into the insulated carafe (which comes with a spillproof lid), add ice, and you're good to go!

The bad: It's rather large (technically it IS portable, but this is not something you could transport easily while in a car, etc.; as others have mentioned, it does tend to leak and there are issues with the fine mesh filter). As with any homemade cold brew, it's not fast...but you get several servings from one carafe, and over the long run the Asobu has saved me a lot of money as an iced coldbrew from a major coffee chain can easily run $4 a cup.

It's a great solution if you you have the time and counter / fridge space to make ahead, but does require some advance planning.

Three good things...and the one knife to own. Santoku knives are currently very trendy in the foodie world. One only need watch Food TV for one or two shows to see the myriad of TV chefs that use the santoku (Japanese for three good things) to slice, dice, chop, and scoop ingredients into the bowl.

Traditionally used as a chef's knife in Japan, the hollow granton edge creates extra pockets of air that prevent thin or soft slices from sticking to the blade. The knife has an excellent balance and a heavy weight in the hand. I would recommend using the Wusthof ceramic sharpener to restore the blade to its factory-original sharpness. Wusthof's Classic Santoku is expensive, but a worthwhile investment for your kitchen.

An essential for frosting and layer cakes. If you're a baker who frequently makes brownies, bar cookies, and cakes, you need to have an offset stainless-steel icing spatula in your collection. The blade is the ideal combination of strength and flexibility, and using an offset spatula means that you don't end up dragging your knuckles through your frosting as you work around a cake. It's useful for leveling brownie and cake batters to ensure even baking and is a must-have for spreading frosting, particularly on quick-setting sheet cakes like Texas cocoa cake. It's also my tool of choice for spreading fillings and frosting layer cakes. When you're finished, you can either hand-wash or pop it in the dishwasher.

Small but mighty, this has become my favorite Staub!. I own a number of Staub cocottes in various shapes and sizes including the pumpkin, tomato, and oval, so when I heard that Staub had come out with a rice cooker modeled on the Japanese hagama that can cook rice in only 20 minutes, I was intrigued.

I've used a Zojirushi rice cooker for the last seven years, but it takes an hour to make even one cup of white rice, so I loved the idea of a stovetop rice cooker that only takes 10 minutes of active cooking time (plus steaming and soaking).

I tested out the petite French oven making white (sushi) rice, the tomato risotto recipe from Staub Japan's site, and the bacon and mushroom rice. First, rinse and soak your rice for 30 minutes. Next, add the rice and fresh water to the cocotte. Bring to a rapid boil (until small bubbles come up around the edges). Stir everything well, cover, reduce the heat to low and simmer for 10 minutes. Remove from heat and allow to steam for 10-15 minutes (longer steaming equals fluffier rice!).

Rice comes out perfectly every time and the petite French oven makes an attractive serving dish as well. I have several petite ovens in different colors including sapphire and la mer, and they are also fantastic for dips, soups, fondues and anytime you don't feel like hauling out a larger pot. It's great for dinners for one or two or reheating leftovers too!

Make your home into a vampire-free zone!. For years, I used my [[ASIN:B00004OCJX OXO Good Grips Garlic Press]] on a weekly basis until one sad day, the metal hinge broke right across the top. Because of the design flaw (other reviewers have had the exact same experience with the metal buckling), I wanted a replacement that didn't have the hinge at a pressure point. I also *didn't* want something like Zyliss's [[ASIN:B00004T14B Zyliss Susi DeLuxe Garlic Press]], where the paint comes off on your garlic.

I narrowed down my choices to the [[ASIN:B000063Y8F Rösle Garlic Press]] garlic press and the Kuhn Rikon, both designed in Switzerland and manufactured in (where else?!?) China. Both are made of stainless steel and are dishwasher safe. I tried out the Rosle at a Williams-Sonoma and was unimpressed by the lightweight feel of the handles, so I took my chances with the Kuhn Rikon (rated "best garlic press" by the illustrious Cook's Illustrated). The handles are also ergonomic and great for arthritis suffers like myself. At more than twice the cost of my old press, it was a lot more than I wanted to spend, but I also didn't want to throw away money on a cheap model that I'd end up replacing sooner rather than later.

I took it for a test drive on some particularly large cloves of garlic. The Epicurean demolished it on the first squeeze, and rather messily, I might add. Remember those slo-mo videos of a bullet going through an apple? Imagine all those little garlic particles spraying all over your stove. You get the picture. I aimed a little more carefully on the second clove, and voila. The press literally used up 99% of the garlic clove, unlike my previous Oxo, which would leave about 30% still intact. The swinging basket design makes cleanup a breeze; no tool is included, but you just need to dig out the remains with a fingernail or toothpick and rinse. It's dishwasher-safe and has a lifetime warranty. Although it's probably the priciest kitchen utensil I've invested in, I use *a lot* of fresh garlic and need something that can live up to the hype.

Five stars for versatility, four stars for plastic and fflimsy rubber. I waded through a myriad of blender reviews before settling on the Oster 6-in-1 Stainless Steel Blender. We used to have a vintage Oster beehive blender from the 1960s, so I knew that it was a brand with a good reputation. The biggest appeal of the 6-in-1 is its versatility: besides the blender jug, it also comes with a milkshake blade and stainless milkshake pitcher, food processor, and baby food jar.

The motor drive is metal, and the blender base is stainless, with a very solid weight to it. So many of the other blenders I researched had plastic gears and components and looked as if they'd break the first time I used them. With 550 watts, this is more like a jackhammer that quickly and effectively makes short work of ice cubes. There are only three basic speeds, and I've found that pulsing works best, as the motor may work overtime when you're only blending a small amount. Unlike some reviewers, I didn't find the Oster's motor to be as noisy as claimed.

I've used it to make milkshakes and breakfast smoothies (ice cubes, almond milk, yogurt and frozen berries), and also used the included food processor attachment to make a small batch of artichoke dip (artichoke hearts, garlic, lemon juice and mayo). I have many recipes that will make good use of these additional features. This is a good deal for the money, as it is capable of more than simply blending. I only wish that some of the additional components were built of a sturdier plastic (the rubber gaskets are flimsy as well).

Durable AND beautiful. I'm a dedicated (amateur) home baker who bakes several times a week, and there are two final frontiers still unknown to me: yeast breads and fancy layer cakes. Unlike simple Bundt cakes or single-layer cakes, layer cakes are composed of two (usually three) or more layers of carefully arranged cakes glued together with some sort of icing (fudge, chocolate, buttercream, etc.). If you're trying to assemble and frost a layer cake on a stationary cake stand, it's much harder to achieve a smooth finish when frosting the outside as you have to keep manually turning the stand, which can cause the cake to wobble and become crooked as you're trying to ice it.

I decided to take the plunge and invest in an Ateco revolving cake stand. It has a very solid cast iron base with a lovely vintage white finish and a 1/8" aluminum top. It also comes with a nonstick pad that can either be used under the stand to keep it anchored to the countertop, or on top of the stand to stabilize your layer cake.

There are several different companies (Magic Line, Wilton, Ateco) that manufacture similar cast iron revolving cake stands, but I chose Ateco based on prior brand purchases (cake decorating equipment) and the fact that the stand is constructed in the USA (other than Nordicware, Libbey and Anchor, it's increasingly difficult to find items made in-country!). It came highly recommended by America's Test Kitchen as well. The packaging was very secure and I received my stand without any scratches or dents.

This is a hefty stand, both in weight and cost, that will stand up to a lifetime of use and is well worth the investment if you're a professional baker, pastry chef, or a home cook who makes a lot of layer cakes. If you're just a casual layer cake baker, consider Ateco's US-made plastic revolving stand for 2/3 less. But this is the rare piece of kitchen equipment that is not only useful, but aesthetically pleasing as well; I leave mine displayed on my baker's rack when not in use.

If you're looking for starter ideas for layer cakes, some of my favorites are [[ASIN:1580085628 The Pastry Queen: Royally Good Recipes from the Texas Hill Country's Rather Sweet Bakery & Cafe]] by Rebecca Rather (Texas-inspired layer cakes and baked goods), [[ASIN:1584797215 Baked: New Frontiers in Baking]][[ASIN:0609604538 Kaffeehaus: Exquisite Desserts from the Classic Cafés of Vienna, Budapest, and Prague]] (Matt Lewis and Renato Poliafito), and Kaffeehaus (Rick Rodgers).

Sleek and streamlined stainless kettle. I had a faithful KitchenAid tea kettle for many years, until it finally rusted and became unusable, so I was looking for a replacement for making hot water for tea and other beverages.

In the past, I have owned several Kenmore appliances, but did not realize that they also made a line of housewares as well, so I was curious to try out the Kenmore Halsted tea kettle.

Out of the box, I was struck by the streamlined, modern appearance. It felt quite hefty upon picking up, and once filled with water, heated evenly and quickly and cleaned up like a breeze.

It also looks quite nice with any kitchen decor.

The only change I would like to see would be for it to have a metal handle assembly rather than a plastic one, but other than that, it works as intended and looks fashionable doing so.

I'd previously ordered the NordicWare Bee Cookie stamps and loved them, and the Starry Night cookie stamps don't .... I ordered these after seeing them featured on King Arthur Flour's website; I'd previously ordered the NordicWare Bee Cookie stamps and loved them, and the Starry Night cookie stamps don't disappoint. The three gorgeous Nordic-inspired designs will be sure to dress up your holiday baking; they work particularly well with gingerbread (there is a recipe included on the box; I opted to use King Arthur Flour's Winter Spice recipe (see comment below).

Be sure to wash the stamps thoroughly the first time before use, and to dry thoroughly; it's normal to see a light layer of grey come off. Do not submerge the wooden handles in water.

It took a few tries to get the hang of using these; one recipe recommended rolling out the dough to 1/4', stamping, then cutting, but I opted to roll the dough into 1-oz. balls, rolled in sugar, then stamped.

Be sure to use a nonstick spray and/or flour your stamps generously between cookies. Stamp until you can see the edge of the dough peek out from under the stamp, then I found that twisting and lifting, the stamps separated easily.

Once cookies were baked and cooled, I used Wilton Pearl Luster mixed with ginger liqueur to paint the tops, and they are gorgeous enough to be hung on a Christmas tree and make a stunning addition to your cookie tray.

How to have a real "can-do" attitude!. Having gone through a procession of can openers, I was tired of ineffective can openers that a) did a poor job of cutting through the lid b) were constantly dirty from being splashed by the can's liquid contents, and c) slicing myself open on lids when taking out the trash. In addition, I also have arthritis in my hands and recurring tendonitis in my left wrist, so the top-down squeezing motion put uncomfortable pressure on my joints.

Exasperated, I finally went out and bought the Oxo Safety Can Opener, and have fallen head over heels in love. Here's why: first, like most Oxo kitchen tools, the handles are covered in a nonslip, easy to wash material. The knob is large, ergonomic, and coated in the same nonslip material. It offers little resistance, so it is easy to turn. Second, instead of the traditional can opener design that requires you to squeeze the handles together, the Oxo features parallel handles that lock together, so there is minimal pressure required.

The best feature is the fact that the lid is cut from the side, so you are not puncturing the can and forcing liquid to splash out, so the gears stay clean (especially beneficial when opening sticky liquids like condensed milk and dulce de leche). In fact, you don't ever see the gears as they cut, and it's initially easy to think that the can opener isn't doing anything. Another great feature is the nifty set of metal pincers that stick out from the side--these grab onto the lid and allow you to separate it from the can without having to touch it (and yes, the lid comes off as smooth as the sample lid packaged with the can opener).

The days of struggling with cheap, difficult to use can openers are over. No more splashed liquid (eau de tuna, anyone?), strained hands, or nasty cuts from too-sharp edges and spurs left behind. For those with arthritis, this is the perfect space-saving solution to buying an expensive electric can opener.

Total gamechanger, even if you own other Zojirushi rice cookers. Even though I could have purchased the same model locally in Japan for much less, I made the choice to purchase a Zojirushi made for the US market (120 v). This was important to me for a number of reasons: not only for the convenience of having English menus and documentation, but also the fact that rice cookers in Japan run on 100v, and unless used with a step-down transformer, can burn out much more quickly on US voltage. Since I make rice almost daily, I wanted a rice cooker that would work in both Japan as well as the US and one that offered a number of functions.

So when I had the chance to test out Zojirushi’s updated Umami model (NL-GAC10) I jumped at the chance. Not only does it have settings like jasmine, quick jasmine, sushi, mixed rice and brown rice, but it also has a setting just for quinoa and Zojirushi’s exclusive umami mode, which soaks the rice longer to produce a moist, fluffy rice. The Umami model also comes with a steamer basket, making it easy to quickly steam veggies, fish, or eggs and create a complete meal.

I love the fact that it has settings not found on other rice cookers, particularly the GABA brown rice setting. GABA brown rice is sprouted brown rice that is much higher in gamma-aminobutyric acid and fiber and is said to be more easily digestible. It requires a long soaking and heating process (using the GABA Brown Rice setting activates the GABA in the brown rice by soaking it for two hours at 104°F before cooking), but the resulting rice is fluffy, moist, and flavorful. And those looking for traditional breakfast options like congee or okayu will find special modes for those as well. Another unique feature is the “slow cook” setting, which lets you make soups and stews right in the rice cooker, and the rewarming feature to bring cooked rice to the perfect serving temperature.

The timer function makes it easy to have perfect rice ready and waiting in the morning to make bento boxes, or have dinner ready when you get home (takikomi gohan is a favorite in my household).

I put the Umami Micom through its paces making several batches of umami, sushi rice, GABA brown rice, mixed rice, and basmati rice cooked on the jasmine setting, as well as following Zojirushi’s recipe for slow cooker minestrone and caprese rice salad. You’ll also find a wealth of other great recipes on their website at https://www.zojirushi.com/app/recipe/rice-cookers and Just One Cookbook’s website.

The Zojirushi Umami micom rice cooker is incredibly versatile; whether you’re shopping for your first Japanese rice cooker or an appliance that can handle a variety of tasks from steaming to slow cooking to making perfect white, brown, jasmine, and sushi rice, the Zojirushi Umami Micom (available in 5.5 and 10-cup size) is the perfect all-in-one appliance, especially if your family eats rice or grains daily.

Essential for kitchen prep. Wusthof's Pull Apart Shears would be my one "desert island" necessity: I use them for snipping fresh herbs such as mint, basil and rosemary, snipping macerated fruit into smaller pieces, cutting parchment paper to fit pans, making quick work of coarsely chopping pecans and walnuts, and chopping vegetables such as asparagus into uniform lengths. Avoid cheap imitations...Bodum Chambord is the *original* French press. As the Bodum box says, "Give up bad coffee for good!". The French press has been around for decades in Europe, an easy alternative to pricier espresso machines and Italian stovetop Moka pots. Bodum is the foremost name in quality French press pots (styles include the Chambord, Brazil, Kenya, and Eileen), and the Chambord is the flagship line, available in 3, 4, 8, and 12 cups.

*NOTE*: the "cups" listed on the box refers to the *European* 4-oz. espresso cup, not a 6- or 8-oz. U.S. cup, so the U.S. measurements are: 3 cup = 1.5 U.S. (12 oz.), 4 cup = 2 U.S. (16 oz.), 8 cup = 4 U.S. (32 oz.) and 12 cup = 6 U.S. (48 oz.).

The Chambord press is simple, efficient, and stylish, and most importantly, solidly constructed. Made of a borosilicate beaker and chromed brass with a molded handle, with proper care, it will last for years. Parts are dishwasher safe, but I prefer to hand wash. There are a number of cheap, made-in-China imposters to be found in discount kitchen stores, but these do not compare to the Portuguese-made originals.

Because the French press takes a coarser grind and doesn't use a paper filter, this allows the coffee's oils and essences to be extracted 100% for a full-bodied, intense brew reminiscent of espresso. Unflavoured dark roasts yield the best results.

To make the perfect cup of French press coffee, use one Bodum scoop (2 Tbsp, included) per 4-oz. cup of coffee (coarse grind ONLY). Add hot, not boiling water, stir with a chopstick or plastic spoon, and put the lid on (with the filter pulled to the top in the closed position). Do not press down. Allow grounds to steep for four minutes. Leaving the spout in the closed position, grasp the handle firmly with the spout pointed away from you. Using the flat of your hand, push the handle down *slowly and evenly* (if you shove the handle down, there is a chance that scalding coffee may shoot out!) until the filter is at the bottom of the carafe. Pour and enjoy. Be sure to thoroughly clean the filter after each use. Replacement carafes and filter parts are available from Bodum's website, [...] Say goodbye to stale, bland coffee; take the plunge (bad French press pun intended!) with Bodum's Chambord and see what you've been missing!

Hefty in the hand, the pastry scraper is a substantial weight with an ergonomic handle that makes it easy to hold onto. However, the blade is lethally sharp; be particularly cautious if you're chopping something hard like carrots where the blade is likely to bounce or slip; a trip to the emergency room might result (haven't had it happen with this, but two of my (klutzy) family members sliced themselves open on the [[ASIN:B000AREB5S OXO Good Grips Mango Splitter]] blade). Bakery-quality bread at home. A family member purchased the Cuisinart CBK 200 Convection Bread Maker and loved its ease of use and excellent results. After a recent move to San Antonio, I was given my own Cuisinart Bread Maker as a gift, and make a minimum of two loaves every week.

The Cuisinart CBK 200 is easy to use: simply remove the pan, attach the kneading paddle, and add ingredients in the order listed. You can choose between a 1, 1 ½, and 2 pound loaf, and from 16 dough settings, including dough, quick bread/cake, gluten-free, low-carb, whole wheat, artisan, sweet bread, and even jam (jam recipes are included). Three crust settings (light, medium, and dark) are available depending on your taste. Cleanup is a breeze: after the loaf has been removed from the pan, simple wash the pan and paddle in hot soapy water.

The included recipe booklet is more than adequate as a starting point for novice bread bakers, and includes detailed instructions on how to measure ingredients, the correct temperature of liquids, and troubleshooting tips. Recipes cover a wide range: sweet breads such as Panettone (Italian Christmas loaf), sour cream chocolate tea loaf, and carrot cake, savory breads (Gruyere and walnut wheat, blue cheese and olive), and artisan loaves finished in the oven. I have tried close to a dozen of the included recipes, and all turned out marvelously. The book also includes a nice selection of low-carb and gluten-free breads.

The only downside is the inability to reset options once "start" has been pushed. The unit has a 15-minute power failure memory, but if you wait 15 minutes to reset your yeast will likely not rise properly since the liquids will have cooled. Another tip is that breads which contain a lot of sugar (such as sweet bread) are more likely to have a dark crust, so you may want to choose the lightest crust setting instead of medium as suggested in the included recipe booklet.

The Cuisinart Bread Maker comes with a generous 3-year warranty, so be sure to register online. This is a wonderful gift for the home baker, with easy, reliable results that rival loaves from your local bakery.

Skip the gourmet coffeeshop and make your own drinks at home!. My very first espresso maker about 20 years ago was a DeLonghi - It was quite basic but did the job well. After many years of faithful service, my replacement Gaggia gave up, so I was looking for an espresso machine that could provide ample pressure (and a grinder). Upon unboxing, I was impressed by the solid build quality and overall looks of the La Specialista; is it gorgeous on the countertop and has a bit of a 1950s vibe to it.

Pros: Two independent heating systems (one for milk, one for coffee). You can tamp directly in the filter holder. The advanced latte system lets you choose between flat (hot milk only) or foam. It has three presets for espresso, Americano, and coffee.

Be sure to read the instruction manual before attempting setup. It's worth watching all the DeLonghi how-to videos on YouTube first before setting up for the first time (especially about using the built-in grinder as this is my first machine that has one, and there's definitely a bit of a learning curve). And you may want to experiment with the coffee bean grinder (any whole coffee beans will work; it doesn't have to be "espresso" blend!) to find the grind that's best for you.

This is like upgrading to a Ferrari; absolute beauty! I loved the quick startup (my previous Gaggia took about 10 minutes to prime) and the quality of the crema / coffee (if you are a fan of flavored drinks, you can also make your own mochas or add flavored syrups; I loved the fact that this makes fantastic flat whites). Absolutely gorgeous foam, too.

Overall, I'm absolutely thrilled with the La Specialista and look forward to many years of excellent lattes and cappuccinos!

Another excellent kitchen tool from Oxo. I own close to two dozen OXO kitchen products, from the can't-live-without-it [[ASIN:B0000CCY1Y OXO Good Grips 3-Piece Angled Measuring Cup Set]] to single-use items that don't see much daily use ([[ASIN:B000AREB5S OXO Good Grips Mango Splitter]]). I own a couple of other OXO whisks, but this is my first OXO silicone whisk.

As I cook and bake several times a week, good whisks are important for me. The silicone coating is heat-resistant up to 600 degrees, so it can be used on pans taken straight from the oven, and is safe on Teflon and other nonstick coatings. As with other OXO products, the nonslip handle makes it easy to grab, even with wet hands. The wires are flexible enough to mix thick batters effectively, but sturdy enough that they don't lose their shape (I've owned several whisks with wires so bendable that they practically folded flat as soon as you went to use them). And it's dishwasher-safe, so I just throw it into the dishwasher when I'm done.

In short, this is another winner from OXO that I find myself reaching for on a regular basis. If you don't mind paying a little extra, I highly recommend my all-time favorite silicone balloon whisk, [[ASIN:B0000DHGE5 Le Creuset 10-Inch Silicone Balloon Whisk, Cherry]] (which was still made in the USA the last time I purchased one), but for the price, the OXO silicone balloon whisk does a fine job and is super-easy to clean.

Ease of use, attractive design and compact size make this Bodum grinder an attractive addition to any kitchen. Being a coffee lover, I prefer to grind my coffee beans immediately before brewing my coffee. This Bodum bistro blade grinder is the third grinder I have used in my kitchen. It is very basic, yet stylish. One of the design elements liked and appreciated are the raised dot area which ensures a slipproof grip. Another nice feature is the recess at the bottom of the grinder which allows the cord to be stored and out of the way.

This is a very basic unit but it gets the job done with a minimum of fuss. There are no additional settings so it is a good unit for the "grinding impaired". The lid is transparent so you have a visual of the grind and can determine the fineness at a glance. All you need to do is press down (a maximum of 60 seconds at a time) on the push-button control until you have the desired grind for your type of brewing. I use a drip-style pot so can't comment on the consistency and quality of espresso grind.

I would like to point out that I did encounter a minor problem when using the grinder for the first time. After grinding the beans, I emptied the ground coffee into the transparent cap where some of the "coffee dust" settled under the push-button control. This prevented the control from working. Once I figured out the problem, I simply removed the powdery residue and everything worked fine.

From my experience with blade coffee grinders, they all operate on the same basis with good results. The ease of use, attractive design and compact size of this Bodum make it an attractive addition to any kitchen.

Very good basic bread maker. My very first bread maker was the similar-looking Cuisinart CBK-100, which was a faithful workhorse until the dough bucket fell apart out of warranty (and a replacement would have cost as much as a new bread maker).

I loved the various modes (sweet bread, gluten-free, jam, artisan, dough mode only) and used it several times a week.

So when I had the opportunity to review the Hamilton Beach Premium Dough & Bread Maker Machine with Auto Fruit and Nut Dispenser, 2 lb. Loaf Capacity, I was eager to get back into breadmaking. The Hamilton Beach offers three different loaf sizes (1, 1.5 and 2 pounds) and crust settings, 14 presets for bread, dough, jam and cake, automatic fruit and nut dispenser, and a dishwasher-safe pan. One feature I really liked not present on my other bread makers is the "rise" setting that is meant for use with frozen bread dough. I would have liked to see more sample recipes in the included booklet (I still have my older Cuisinart manual as it has about 40 recipes that all work like a charm sized for 1, 1.5 and 2-pound loaves!).

In looks and setup, it is very similar to the Cuisinart (including the viewing window on top). Do be very careful to always use oven mitts when handling the pan because it gets HOT (as does the outside of the machine; be sure not to push it up against a wall as the convection fan needs air to circulate).

Similar to my Cuisinart, though, I'm not thrilled about the baking performance (I prefer to use the machine on dough mode and finish baking in the oven) as I find bread machines tend to bake unevenly (and never get as crispy as I like for artisan doughs, which I always finish in the oven).

But for everyday use and for kneading and mixing doughs, the Hamilton Beach is more than up to the task and I look forward to experimenting with bread machine recipes from some of my other cookbooks.

Impressive for the price. I've had this popper for a couple of weeks, wanted to wait until I'd used it to review.
